RAYMOND A. EBBA GE
A "Good Guy," A Dreamer, A Fighter, A Leader. A Patriot, A Mason.

RAYMOND A . EBBAGE
Grand Master
October 12, 1973 - October 17. 1974

Each is a n appropriate description of Raymond A. Ebbage, the I 08th
M. · .W. ·.Grand Master of Masons in California and Hawaii.
He was born March 20th. 1913, in Vancouver. British Columbia, and then
orphaned at an early age. Ray shortly thereafter came to California to reside with
relatives .
He received his education in the public schools of California. graduated from
San Francisco's Polytechnic High School. and then majored in accounting at the
University of San Francisco.
With his coming of age. and. having objective ly studied the governments of
several countries. Ray applied for and received citizenship in the United States. He
is justly proud of having become an American and has never regretted his decision.
On October 17, 1937 , Ray married his lovely wire Ruth. They are the proud
parents of a daughter, Elgeane and a son, Donald. and have been blessed with four
grandc hildren.
During World War II, he fel t it his obligation to be of serv ice to his adopted
country, and he volunteered for duty as a Private in the Infantry of the United
States Anny. His leadership qualities qu ickly qualified him for a commission. He
saw action in the European Theater as a Captain (Infantry Company Commander)
and. as a result of his outstandingly courageous actions. received the Silver Star.
the Bronze Star with Cluster, and France's Croix de Guerre.
On returning home to Sacramento. Brother Ray returned to the insurance business and, in due time, earned the designation of Chartered Life Underwriter. He
also became a past president of the Life Managers Association . His professional
career has remained with insurance and, for the past several years, he has been the
General Agent in the Greater Sacramento Area for a large life insurance company.
In his Masonic career. he received the Degree of Master Mason on February 17.
1950. in Capital City Lodge No. 499. and, in 1957, served as Master. Since
then. his Masonic endeavors have been tireless. In addition to being the Senior
Grand Deacon in 1962, he has served as a member of the Public Schools Committee, the Sojourners Committee, the Constitution Observance Committee, the
DeMolay Liaison Board, and on the Board of Trustees o f the California Masonic
Memorial Temple a nd the Masonic Homes of California.
Venerable Master of the Lodge of Perfection of the Sacramento Scottish Rite
Bodies in 1968. he was decorated with the rank and t itle of Knight Commander of
the Court of Honor in 1969. He is also a member of the Sacramento York Rite Bodies , Sciots' Tract Pyramid No. 11 of the AEOS. Ben Ali Temple of the Shrine.
Sacramento Court No. 119 of the Royal Order of Jesters, and Sacramento Chapter
No. 133 of the National Sojourners. In 1967 he served as President of the Northern
California Past Masters Association. He is a member of St. Francis Conclave of
the R ed Cross of Constantine, and has rece ived the Honorary Legion of Honor
award of the Order o f DeMolay. In each of the organizations of which he is a
member. he has taken an active role in pursuing its objectives and programs .

In 1970, our Brother was e lec ted to the office of Junio r Grand Warden, a nd served with distinction therein and in eac h of the succeeding offices. c ulminat ing with
his installation as Grand Master in October 197 3. His installation was the first in
the history of our Grand Lodge where the general membership, with fam ilies and
friends, were invited to be present. The event was cond ucted with all the dignity
that be fib such an occasion and was inspiring to all who attended .
During his travel s a.s G rand Master, Brother Ray was particularly ple ased to
attend the programs of the smaller and more remote Lodges of our Grand
Juri!>dict ion. Notable among them were the Centen ni al celebrations of seven o f
our Lodges: Athem, No. 228, Janesville No. 232. Calistoga No. 233, Hope No.
234, Surprise Valley No. 235, Hills Ferry No. 236 , and Guada lupe No. 237.
Ray's visits to Janesvill e No. 232 and Surprise Valley No. 235 were of particular
Masonic pleasure to him. they being the first time in the history of these Lodges
tha t the Grand Master had been present at the ir meet ings.
He took great pleas ure in wearing the gleaming white Stetson hat give n to him
in testimony of his bei ng one o f the "good guys." His relationship to his
Brethren throughout the year more than confirmed this designation.
Always a salesman, o ur Brother, on every proper occasion, took time and effort to encourage our members to be "salesmen'· of Masonry-by proudly wearing the Square and Compass (the most widely known and respected fraternal
emblem in the world); by eac h of us displaying , through our perso nal actions ,
o ur conviction in the value of the tenets of Masonry; and, by so refl ecting the
merits of our teachings we can convince others of the good of o ur Institution .
Ou r Grand Master s pent much effort in bringing proper instruction to the Craft
a s co its moral and spiritual behavior- perhaps no thing more so than in the
cardinal points he repe atedly stressed: a dedication to God, personal integri ty.
family unity , and parental responsibility. Each of these was a natural outgrowth
of Ray's personal life and belief-and worthy of o ur imitation . To these was
added hi s recognition of the good in every person and every thing; he enjoyed
"looking for the good. and praising it."
On other occasions . o ur leader, feeling a far mo re patriotic responsibility than
some of us , ex.pounded on the duties , responsibil ities and privileges of being an
Americ an . Receiving the Freedom Foundation ' s Gold Medal Award in 1970 fo r
his speech o n "Our Flag, " he continued throughout his Grand Lodge Line offices w ith a sincere emphasis, upon every occasion, to remind us of the great
heritage that is ours in this great country-and, of our responsibi lity in continuing its existence through respect for our Flag and true involvement, at every
level , in o ur Government.
Ever the dreamer, Ray dreamt. but al so put his shoulder to the wheel to
promote the greatness of o ur Country and the advancement of Freemaso nry in it.
As in his wartime leadership, th ose who worked closely with Ray during his
tenure in the office of Grand Master fo und him to be the kind they would follow
into battle, without question. Though always demanding of him~elf, hi s tole rance for the defic iencies and weaknesses of others was laudable.
His judgment in matters of policy, his tact and discretion in handling the multitudinous items of concern to the Grand Master, will , for many years. be
rerJected in the growth and stature of our Gra nd Lodge , a nd of Masonry in
general throughout California and Hawaii .

I have enjoyed many conversations with him concerning the philosophy, teachings and purposes of Masonry . He is God inspired and moves from one goal to
the next to produce all the good that he can.
I also thank the members of Grand Lodge for their encouragement as I

Yes. People are funny and they do need help. In my life time 1 have never seen so

today. They see the worst in everything and everybody including themselves .
Solomon is recorded in Proverbs 23:7 stating a natural law of the Universe
concerning one's thinking:
"As a man thinketh in his heart so is he." In practical language it rnn be
expressed this way : Everyone' s life is a sum total of his or he r thinking
and doing. If you constantly think abou t bad things . you'll get more of
the same. The law is this . . . you create in life what you think about.
Another law that is vital to the good life you want to live is this:
If you do not appreciate the good you have you will lose it. For example, if
you do not appreciate and take care of your material things such as a house. a car
or a watch you will lose them. You can lose family and friends the same way .
And this is true of our country and all of itssedomes. Since about 1930 there

tum the tide tow ard seeing the good in o ur country and people.
I propose a slogan for this purpose : "SEE THE GOOD AND PRAISE IT."
See the good in all people. Do not over-react to people and situations; See the
good in free enterprise; See the good in our Departments of Government. Of
course, our people, business and Government processes are not perfec t, but I
give this warning. YOU CAN'T BUILD GOOD OUT OF THE BAD . You can
only build good out of the good. LOOK FOR THE GOOD AND PRAI SE IT.

of t hemselves CIS being faces and blame other people and bad economic
conditions. All of them think that life is somethin g for nothing, but soon I make

they must live in accord with the laws of the Universe that involve their lives.
I teach them to be aware of two C1spects of reality. First, that the laws of the
Universe are stable and constant. Second. that forms are always changing. This
is the basis of living and a good life. Learn to use various laws to produce certain
good things and they will always work for you in that given way. As you learn to
chose how to use various laws, you can change your.;elf and condit ions to fulfill
your desires.
Through the Law of cause and effect. what thought has created. thought c an
change. You think and c hange the cause and thus change the effect. The first law

GOOD AND PRAISE it.

When I began my thrilling tour last October with Grand Lodge I was often
asked what attracted me to Masonry. It was the word' Architect' used to desc ribe
God. At that time my oldest daughter was very ill and I needed to rum to a Power
greater th an myself fo r guidance and strength. Up to that time God was a very
nebulous thing to me, but when a Masonic friend told me that God was the
'Architect" and C reator of the Universe, including a ll people and things, my life
was strengthe ned.
Since then I have studied the subject and I'd like to present it fo r yo ur
consideration.
It is not known how or when the word 'Arc hitect' came to be used in
describing the C reative Power of the Universe. Howeve r. the word 's etymology
provides a clue regarding why the word would be applied to the Div.inc Power of
Creation . The first four letters , ·arch ,' originally referred to a solid geome tric
fonn very commonly used in construction: a curved structura l de~ice use? to ~.ro­
vide suppon . T he Greek word ' arch' is pnnced 'ar-hee ' meaning, chief, hrst
or beginning. The last ponion of the word, ' tect' was taken from the Greek woi:d
'tekh ne' whic h meant art or skill. Therefore, when the two words are placed m
conj unction, o ne is actually describing an entity possessed of the greatest or most
eminent skill .
Masonic history does not explain why the attributes of the human architect
were adopted to describe and show respect for God. But by imagining th~ experiences of early Maso nic workmen and architects, it becomes clear and logical.
The first architec ts had little knowledge to draw from . Few people could read
or write and there were very few words and sy mbols. This made it next to

impossible to pass knowledge on from one generation to the next. Kno.,.,..ledge
was preserved ma inly through the experience of using the known build ing tools
such as the square . compass. le vel and the plumb line. One generation would
overlap the next. so knowled ge of the building trade was preserved .
We know that the cornerstone was the beginning. o f a building. Through geometry the floor. walls and roof were calcu lated from it. As the arch itect and
workmen labored on a building, they soon disco\'ered that the laws of mathemati cs demanded that the workmen wo rk togethe r in harmony and
responsibility . If they did not, the building would soon fall down and they wou ld
lose their trade . None of the builders co uld allow big mistak es or bad work to be
done.
This caused the architect and workme n to fo nn a philosophy of liv ing. T hey
reaso ned that the laws of the Unive rse and of building were stable and therefore
responsible. This being tru e, experie nce showed them that they must correspo nd
to the laws they worked with . So brotherly love, relief. truth and fortitude are not
j ust good ideas but are laws of the uni verse .
This probably was the firs t light of understanding for Masons, that there was a
connection between the work they did a nd the laws of the Uni verse. As time
went on, the workmen began to wonder how the archi tect fou nd out abOut the
building tools, and from where d id he obtain the plans of architecture for eac h
building.
When they asked the Architect. he maybe wa' at first a little bewildered,
because it seemed to just come to him.
'' i son of just think to myse lf" he could have said, " I plan what I want to do
and then 1 figure our how to do it." Thi~ is what is called M EDITATION or talk·
ing with God the Architect and Creator.
The bu ilders· soon showed great respect for th e Architec t because he seemed
to be the source of all ideas that gave them work . This respect, in time. caused
the a rchitects to inquire of themselves . .. " Where does all th is knowle dge .
w isdom and unde rstand ing come from? .. The ir reasonin g m ight have gone like
th is:

9

I pause in peace a nd quiet and I think . Cou ld it be that there is a Great
Arc hitect th at I contact in thought ? It mu~t be an 'all knowing
intelligence .' T hen it seemed logical th at thought and laws of building
or creating were o ne and the same .
Many Masons and others ha ve now logically determined that Go<l, T he Great
Architect, is Infinite Life and Intelligence in and through all people and things.
Also considerable tho ught has been given to the idea that Infinite Intelligence is
in essence all the laws, rules, regu lations and proce~ses of the Universe. Words
are very lacking in explaining what God is. but a Contemporary Philosopher.
Eme~t Holmes. stated it simpl y and well:
..God is limitl ess Life and Mind and th is Life a nd Mind return s to the
thinker exactly what he thinb into it and does through it."

HERBERT A. HUEBNER

By Ralph H. Head
On an early morning many years ago. a young Harvard professor stood at a
window of Cragie House in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where George Washington had once head4uartered and gazed out at the sloping lawn and the elms,
wondering if Washington might not also have stood there before. feeling unutterably alone and dejected. The young professor's wife had died three years
before, but he still longed for her because time had not softencJ his grief. "This
cannot go on," Henry Wadsworih Longfellow must have saiJ to himself. Life is
not an empty dream. SudJenly he began to write in a surge of inspiration that
which was to become one of the best loved and most widely read poems of all
times, "The Psalm of Life." It is the seventh and eighth verse s we tum to today
as we honor the memory of Herbert Alloway Huebner whose footprints are the
legacy of Cali fomia Freemasonry.
"Lives of great men al I remind us
We can make our lives sublime,
And departing leave behind us
Footprints on the sands of time.
"Footprints that perhaps another
Sailing o'er life's solemn main.
A forelorn anJ shipwrecked brother,
Seeing may take heart again."

The footprihts of Past Grand Master Herbert Huebner are a legion. They
began with his birth in Washington, D. C., in 1902. They ended in Los Angeles
on March 25, 1974, but their trail is not cast in sand but indelibly in the hearts
aml minds of those who knew and loved him.
His early schooling in Fresno, California. was followed by a law degree at the
University of Southern California and what was to be a brillant career as a patent
lawyer commenced in 1926. In 1925 he married Loma Pierce from which union
came a son. Harlan. who would follow in his father's footsteps as his law partner, in due time as Master of the san1e Lodge, Wilshire Lodge No. 455. and as a
valued contributor to the work of Grand Lodge.
After his raising in Wilshire Lodge and his service as Master in 1944, Herbert
Huebner was appointed to the Grievances Committee which activity was followed by energetic and productive work on the History Committee and as
chairman of the Charters and Public Schools Committees. In October of 1967 he
was elected Junior Grand Warden and thence electively elevated to Grand Master
on October 16, 1970. His biography pub I ished in the proceedings of the annual
communication of the Grand Lodge in 1971 proclaimed him to be "a Mason's
Mason." probably as noble a tribute as may be given a man. His leadership ability was further recognized by his election 10 the chairmanship of the Conference
of Grand Masters in Washington, D. C. When his work as Grand Master

coroneted with the 33rd degree in December of that year. He was a member of
the York Rite Bodies. Red Cross of Constantine, Al Malaikiah Shrine and
member of the Board of Governors of the Shriners Hospital. and a member of the
DeMolay Legion of Honor.
His was a complete life. With his love and Jevotion to his family and his invaluable contribution to Freemasonry came his dedication to his profession , serving on boards and a~ president and chairman of patent law assoc iations. For

took Lincoln's life as a chart fo r hi~ own life . He read law by himself a~ Lincoln
and ~o many other de termined men had t.lonc before.
He supported himself as a surveyor and 4ualified a ~ an Indian Agent an<l wa~
assigned to the State of Washington.
During this period be married his wife. "Ne ll." as we all know her and here
began a long and wonderful marriage. To Nell ant.I her daughter, Cheryl Ann
Cook ant.I Son .• Joseph C. Shell we extend our love and friendship.
When he felt that his study of law was ready for use he returned to California
and worked in the co urt:- a~ a Deputy Probation Officer and then a~ a Court
Clerk, took the bar exam ination and pas:-ed it in 1922.

EULOGY
E ARL WARREN

By Chester MacPhce
Earl Warren, the twenty-third District Attorney o f Alameda County; the nineteenth Attorney General of the State of California; the thirtieth Governor of the
State of California ; and the fourteenth Chief Justice of the United States Supreme
Court was the sixty-ninth Grand Master of Maso ns in Califo rnia and o ur Senior
Past Grand Master.
A member of Sequois Lodge No. 349 of Oakland, California for more than
fifty-four years, he was laid to rest with the heroes in Arlington Ceme tery on July
12, 1974.
Earl Warren was a public servant; dedicated to the service of the public. a man
of strong personal convictions, he answered to himself for his acts .
His great dedication. ho nor, and integrity were of oak and rock and as lasting
as the ages.
In the many public offices Earl Warren filled, he discharged his du ties wi th
outstanding ability and with great devotion to the welfare of the people . As he
saw this duty he never faltered or compromised. His heart contained well springs
of human pity and sympathy .
His singular purity of character, his exactitude, his greatness of heart and
mind ; his love for human kind without limitation of race and creed; his philanthropy and splendid achievements - all of these, my Brethren. constitute a
reco rd which enriches the annals of our state and nation, and, indeed . o ur great
Fraternity of Freemasons everywhere . At all times he gave his strength W the
weak , his substance to the poor, his sympathy to the suffering and his heart to
God.
During the period he served as Governor of California, and prior thereto, Earl
Warren and I were good friend . In 1946. he appointed me a mem ber of the
California State Real Estate Commi ss ion. one of the highest honor~ that could
come to me in my profession. He re-appointed me in 1950. I knew his family
well and des pite his man y frnternal and civic duties. he re~erve d adeq uate ti me to
provide the fatherly leadership and lo ve and affection for his wonderful fam ily .
It was my good fortune as Grand Master in 1969 to be in his own Lodgeroo m
at Sequoia Lodge in Oakland surrounded by the officers of his Lodge and other
well wishers to present him with his 50-year pin .
Indeed. Earl Warren served his beloved Masonic Fraternity with a fervor and
zeal equaled by few. He was one of California's great Grand Mas te r~ .
And now he ha~ gone to labor in the vineyard of eternal life .
Eat:h day mo re than 100.0(X) human feing s finish their earthly existence and
pass into the unknown beyond . It was Job who cried out, "[f a man die . will he

live again?"
My Brethren . life and death are one. Imperceptibly they blend into one
another. Someone once said. ·· 1f there be a design in this world and , indeed . in
this universe. there must be a designer. "

The 1>tate of the Craft ha~ been. with few exceptio ns, hannoniou!> and
progre~s i ve. Authority has generally been administered from the lowest level possible consistent with the problem involved .
California Freemasonry is well-known and envied throughout the worl d .fo r
the ri tua listic perfection of its Officers. Our Ritual Committee has do ne its work
well and is to be hig hly commenued and complimenteu for 1he success atta ined.
Ritual is, and properly should be, of the utm o~t importance during Lodge
meetings . California ritual must be maintained at its prese nt high le vel.
The Master of the indi vidual Lodge bears the respons ibili ty an<l authority to
adminis te r lhe affairs of Masonry within the jurisdiction of his Lodge . However. in
many Lodges there is s uch a singleness of pur[Xlse that ritual has been accepted as
the main purpo~ of their existence. The Master becomes so con~ume<l with the ritualisti c capability of himself and hi s Officers that he overlooks the necessity to rufe
and govern the Lodge over which he is called to preside. Contlicts between
Brethren are ignored or overlookeLI. Good counci l is not whispered . Soothing the
distressed is left to o thers . The widows and orphans arc forgotte n. Brotherly love
and affection become mere phrasing . The exalta1ion to good citizenship is s ile nt.
Freemasonry and its ideal s thus heco me a casualty of s hort-s ighted goals an<l
ambitions. and our image before lhe world becomes tarni shed and tawdry.
Freemasonry is predicated upo n the idea that the individua l is respons ible fo r
his own acts and well-being and that freedom is his <livine righ1, his opportunity ,
and his responsibility. The organization of Freemasonry is to a id and abet the ind ividual in hi!> effort!> toward greater personal development and attainment. ft is not
the organ ization 's function to dic1atorially control his conduct. Thus the duties of
the Master become much more than m ere word perfection or floor work .
To be the Mas ter of a Lodge is a great opportunity for personal growth and
developm ent because in governing and judging the affairs of others. you become
more competent in the administration of yourown. The· 'Wisdom of So lomon· ' is

DUTIES OF GRAND M ASTER

The duties of the Grand Master are getting more.arduous every year. He is
asked personally to make an ever increasing number of public anJ fraternal appearances . A quick look at the schedule of events attended by this Grand Master will
indic ate the time consumed in such affairs anJ the travel involved.
In addition , the Grand Maste r now has every Committee Chainnan , fortyseven in number, reporting to him directly. Each Chairman is thus dependent upon
directions from the Grand Master for the conduct of his Committee. The staffing of
those Committees is a momentous task in itself anJ sho uld be completed by the
time the GranJ Master takes office. The range of Committee activities is so diverse
that adequate familiarity with each Committee's function is nearly impossible.
In addition, every Inspector, under our Masonic Law, is a personal representative of the Grand Master and responsible to him. There are no w 169 Inspectors.
In order to have adequate knowledge of each Inspector and his District the Grand
Master mu st rely o n the Grand Lecturer and the six Assistant Grand Lecturers.
Thus the Grand Master is materially aided in his administrative duties by the Ritual
Committee. However, such is not the case whe re Standing and Special Committees are involved. Some supervisory positions anJ personnel arc needed for Committee control.
I, therefore, recommend that three new executive positions be created for the
supervision and control of the Grand Lodge Committees. Each executive to have a
number of Committee Chairmen reporting to him and he, in tum. reports their
problems and accomplishments to the GranJ Master. The spread of control for the
Grand Master would thus be reduced from forty-seven to three.
The Masonic Homes Endowment Board. under the Chairmanship of Robe rt
E. Hilts, has for the second year in a row exceeded the one million dollar mark in

REIMB l.'RSEME:'-<T OF TRA YEL EXPENSES

The past year has not been kind to our financial picture. Like all organizations
and individuals who have funJs to invest Masonic Lodges in California, and their
Grand Lodge, ha ve been hard hit by the depressed market conditions and by
inflation. It costs mo re to operate and you get less for your money. At the beginning of our last fiscal year the Gr:md Lodge consolidateJ total account was audited
and valued at $40,518,869. The end of the fiscal year shows a total value of
$37,671, 143. The immeJiate future does not promise to be much better. Diligence
and Jue caution have been exercised by the custodians of our funds. The results are
not nearly as bleak as they might have been. The market is down , it will go up. If
we are willing to accept the rewarJs, we must also accept the accompanying risks.
Remember, he who endureth to the end, the same shall be saved. Ever greater
custodial care is being exercised. Faith and hard work will bear fruit and our future
goals will be rnalized. One very bright spot is the complete retirement of all debt
against our California Masonic Memorial Temple in San Francisco. The Temple
Staff, under the leadership of George Gavin, and the Board of Trustees, under
Chaim1an De Wald Baum, are to be highly commended. The returns from their activities are very gratifying.
Travel costs are up materially. Rooms and meals cost more. Old standard s of
re imbursement are inadequate. The allowan ce of ten cents per mile is hardly more
than token repayment and should be increased.
Savings should be effected wherever possible yet curtailment of operations
will only result in fewer and less aJequate services to our membership. That type
of economy should be a voided.
When one of our dedicated me mbers spends time and money in the service of
his Brethren, he sho uld not be asked to sho ulder the entire burden while the inac tive members sit idly by. We should all be willing to share. at least finan cially. in
the costs incurred for such services. I recommend that future standards of
reimbursement be adequate to meet those expenditures. This policy could result in
increased dues or assessments. but the results will generally faroutweigh the cost.

'"As YE Sow. So SHALL YE REAP ..

Mv travels and communications have revealed one very significant fact about
many ~four Brethren. They hold the idea that the lessons and ideals taught in our
Degrees arc purely Masonic and hence•· Secret.'' Such a concept is unhealthy and
injurious. Our ideals and teachings are spelled out in the Holy Bible. They were
taught by Mohammed and Buddha. They arc written into the Declaration of
Independence and the Constitution of these United States. They are fundamental to
man's peaceful coexistence with his family and neighbors. They were given by
God for the benefit of all. Perhaps the most· 'Secret" thing about them is that they
arc so basic and universal that others overlook or fail to recognize them for their
worth. They are thrown into the discards by "the ruthless hand of ignorance."
We have no exclusive right to the practice of brotherly love, relief or truth.
The four cardinal virtues of temperance. fortitude. prudence and justice belong to
all mankind and are hopefully practiced by all.
Freemasonry. however. is distinctly unique from most organizations in that
those virtues are the focal points of all Masonic beliefs and activities. For too long
we have tended to hide our light beneath a bushel in spite of the admonition of that
great Teacher of two thousand years ago. It seems we have placed such a stigma
upon telling others of our ideals that we have, in effect. denied others the privilege
of hearing about or knowing of Freemasonry's ideals and teachings.

If we are ashamed to acknowledge them or admit our commitment to them.
then we should keep them '·Secret.'' If we are ashamed to tell the world about the
virtues we teach and hopefully practice - that we strive for self betterment
th rough learning the Freemason way, that family, fide I ity and parental
responsibility are accepted as necessary to society's existence, that civil obedience
and patriotism are duties for all citizens, that a spiritual commitment to G(xl is the
first duty of all His creatures - then we should practice .. Secrecy." I. personally.
have yet to feel any sense of shame or guilt' for either practicing or preaching the
virtues taught by Freemasonry. It is quite the reverse. When I don ·t practice those
virtues, when [don't strive to maintain those high ideals , then I am ashamed and
try to keep things ··secret.''
I heartily endorse the recommendations and activities of those Past Grand
Masters who have sought to shed greater light before society concerning
Freemasonry and Freemasons. I will even go one step further and recommend that
we re-evaluate our laws, as they specifically relate to publicity and public
relations. in an endeavor to restructure them to properly tell the story of
Freemasonry. its accomplishments and its members to the rest of the world.

Like the famler. we must plant in order to harvest. What we plant we will harvest. However. the challenge must be met and the work must be done before the
rewards are earned. Raising. educating and supervising children is no instant
process.
We, ourselves. have inherited ideals, goals. ambitions. concepts and knowledge. as well as material things, from our forefathers.
We. like our forebears, will bequeath to the future our ideals and attainments.
However. our ideals and attainments will be received and utilized by succeeding
generations in direct proportion to their desire to emulate us.
The youth of our country, our youth, will seek example, guidance and counsel
from someone. If we do not provide them in satisfactory fonn and abundance.
someone else will. It is our great good fortune that we start with all the advantages
on our side. Our children start with us. their parents. as examples. From that time
on we must constantly earn their desire to emulate us.
Many of our Brethren and their wives devote themselves unstintingly and unselfishly to our three Masonic youth organizations - DeMolay. Job's Daughters
and Rainbow for Girls. Many more are needed to provide adequate guidance and
supervision. It is the rare adult who has nothing constructive to offer young people.
For many years the individual Ma~on and his wife have been urged to actively support - physically and financially - the Masonic youth groups. Lodges were
prohibited from supporting them financially.
In J 969 Grand Lodge of California voted to allow Lodge funds to be spent for
the support of Masonic ally affiliated youth organizations. This was a change in the
attitude formerly taken and stressed that the young men of DeMo lay would
probably become Master Masons and should. therefore, be financially supported.
My association with young people indicates that the young women are probahly
the stronger force for future Masonic membership because of their considerable
influence on their husband.~ and the children which they produce.
I cannot emphasize too strongly th e urgent need for the sponsorship of
DeMolay by our Lodges. and your active support of the Job's Daughters and Rain bow groups.

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on By-Laws:
With six members present Saturday morning. October 12th. 197-l: your
Committee on By-Laws began its review of the matter~ referred to it.
Your Committee checked and rechec ked one hundred and fourty-nine B ylaw changes made by the Constituent Lodges ...
All of the reviewed By-Laws amendments and resol utions were fo und to be
in order.
Exhibit A of the Grand Secretary 's Report. to which members of Grand
Lodge may refer. sets forth 143 changes. The six changes approved after said

Change of meeting place: (C.M.C. Sections 372
and 373)---3 Re solutions
Increasing dues (Section 356) 3 Amendments
A Total of 79.
As in the past. your Committee suggests that the Lodges review Article X of
their By-Laws which sets fort h the maximum authority of the Charity Committee
of the Louge during the interval between stated meetings.
Your Committee would like to point out that the charity provision is a ve ry
important part of your By-Laws ant.I a ten dollar amount between statct.I meetings
may not be any charity at all .
Even though all of the amendments reviewed were approved. your Committee fount.I that the matter of t.lesignating holidays in the By-Laws remains
troublesome. Article Ill of the Uniform Code of B y-Laws. which perm its
exception to the regular date of the stated meetings of a Lodge , limits the
exception to legal holidays and during the Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge.
With regard to legal holidays, these shoult.I be specifically named so that
there will be no misunderstanding as to whether a particular day is or is not a
holiday . Furthe r. the particular legal holiday should be identified by NAME and
NOT by date: that is, New Year's is preferable to January I and Independence
Day is preferable to July 4, because such desc ription leaves no dou bt that t he
exception applied when the se days are celebrated on Monday in a year when January l or July .i falls on a Sunday.
Panic ular attention should be paid to this point of designation of holidays.
and especially for Monday night Lodges. By action of Congress , several
holidays will be celebrated on Monday even though they fall o n another day of
the week. All Monday night Lodges should contac t the Grand Secretary' s office
before changing the holidays.
Also a Lodge should provide for an alternate date in case its stated meeting
falls during the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge . While only those
Lodges whose stated meeting is during the second week of the month are affected, the date of any Annual Communication may be changed for any year, so
the contingenc y ~hould be provided for.
In reviewing the re solutions having to do with the change of meeting place
by various Lodges. yo ur Committee found that in several cases a Lodge moved
to a new location without following the formal procedures as set forth in the

California Masoni<.: Code. and when the Lodge notified Grand Lodge it was
mee ting at the ne w location .... uch noti<.:e was the fir:-t knowledge that Grand

have to take the necessary pwi:cdural steps that it ~hould have rnmpleted prior to

TRIAL RECORD No. 2019

This matter was before your Committee last year at which time we
felt that the specifications were not sufficient and recommended that
the matter be returned to the Lodge for correction of the specifications
and retrial. which recommendation was approved by Grand Lodge.
The specifications were redrawn and the matter retried. The specifications and procedures are correct in every detail. The accused, a
member of Indian Wells Valley Lodge No. 691, was charged in two specifications. On the first specification the accused was found not guilty by the Commissioners. On the second specification the accused was charged with cohabiting
in the presence of five minor children with the wife of a Brother Mason prior to
the dissolution of her marriage, prior to her marriage to the accused. The Commission found him guilty of this specification and of un-Masonic conduct and
fixed the penalty at reprimand. Your committee has carefully examined the transcript and trial record and feel that the penalty of reprimand is not sufficient in
the case of a charge as serious as this which affects the image of Masonry in the
community. We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
RESOL YEO: That the finding of guilty of the second specification
and of un-Masonic conduct be approved but that the penalty be raised
to suspension thereby leaving to his Lodge the time when he can be
restored to membership.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2040
A charge of un-Masonic conduct was filed against the accused. a member of
Hawaiian Lodge No. 21, the specifications being that he had conspired to commit bribery, and that he had committed perjury before a Grand Jury. The accused
had previously been convicted by Jury Trial in a United States District Court for
hoth offenses. The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the conviction, and the Supreme Court of the United States denied the accused a petition

TRIAL RECORD No. 2042
The accused, a member of Brooklyn Lodge No. 2:!5, was charged
with a systematic scheme, over the course of years. of filing false
claims resulting in the theft of hundreds of thousands of <lol I ars from
the Medi-Cal program of the State of California.
At trial in- Superior Court for the County of Alameda. the accused
plead guilty to grand theft and was sentenced to the California Medical
Facility, Vacaville, California for the tem1 provided by law.
The accused did not respond to the service of a charge of un-Masonic conduct
from his Lodge.
The Master of Brooklyn Lodge No. 225 investigated the evidence,
found the accused guilty, and fixed the penalty of expulsion.
The record discloses an ahundance of evidence to sustain the
Master's findings and, in the committee's opinion, proper!; fixed the
penalty at expulsion. However, as has occurred in the past, a Trial
Master was not appointed. Because of this irregulurity in procedure,
the matter should be reversed and sent back to th e Lodge for the
Master to secure the valid appointment of a Trial Maqer for his review
and submission of a report to our next Annual Communication.
For reasons heretofore stated, we offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That the action of the Master be reversed and ~et ;,i~ide
and that Trial Record No. 2042 be returned to the Lodge for the
appointment of a Trial Master. that he make his inve~tigation and file a
report at our next Annual Communication.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Grand Lecturer is required at each Annual Communication, to render to
the Grand Lodge, a full and detailed account of his services during the year, and to
set forth therein a report of the condition of the Lodges throughout the Jurisdiction.
I shall very shortly comply with that requirement. Before commencing this report,
however, I beg-your indulgence for one moment, a moment in which to honor the
memory of a former member of this Ritual Committee- Worshipful Wallace H.
Fiske, Assistant Grand Lecturer of Division Four who, in March of this year was
transported upon silent wings to the Celestial Lodge, there to dwell with the other
truly great and good men of Masonry who rest now in Paradise.
It would be impossible to express in.mere words the great admiration and esteem in which Wally was held by all members of this Committee ... He was
gentle; he was friendly; he was true. His quiet and unassuming manner oft times
belied his perfect mastery of the Ritual, and he was loved and respected by all with
whom he came into contact. We take this quiet moment to say farewell to our
Brother - Masonry's benefactor - Wallace H. Fiske, Assistant Grand Lecturer ... To his memory is most lovingly dedicated this report.
Because of the great number of Lodges which are Chartered under the Grand
Lodge of California, it would be impossible for the Grand Lecturer to visit them all
each year. This report, therefore, will be based upon information contained in the
Inspectors Annual report forms, letters and comments from Lodge Officers and
members, and personal observations of the Grand Lecturer after thoughtful consideration of all the above. In a continuing effort toward total uniformity of
California Ritual, many hours, days and weeks have been expended by the Committee on Ritual, the Inspectors, Officers Coaches and Lodge Officers throughout

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the entire Jurisdiction this year. The mainstays of our chain of Ritual instruction
are the Inspectors Annual Spring Conferences. These meetings are held in the
Spring months of each year in each of the Six Divisions . It is at these week-end
long meetings that the Inspectors exemplify all the Ritual of the three degrees in the
presence of the Ritual Committee and the Elective Grand Lodge Officers. This
year, those meetings were held at the locations and the times as follows:

INSPECTORAL CORPS

88

Division One at Santa Rosa, April 19-21, conducted by Wor. Burton Young,
Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division One.
Division Two at Sacramento, June 21-23, conducted by Wor. Edward Seagle,
Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division Two.
Division Three at Los Gatos, March 22-24, conducted by Wor. Ulysses Patropulos, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division Three.
Division Four at Fresno, May 31-June 2, conducted by Wor. Vernon Gordon,
Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division Four.
Division Five at Los Angeles, May 17-19, conducted by Wor. George Perkins,
Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division Five.
Division Six at Long Beach, February 22-24, conducted by Wor. Ernest M. Newton, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division Six.
It is interesting to note that at each of these conferences, all phases of the Ritual were exemplified and discussed within the period commencing Friday evening
and concluding on Sunday morning. This accomplishment is but one further
indication of the studied determination of the Inspectors to maintain high levels of
Ritual proficiency within their individual areas of responsibility.
It was the good fortune of the Inspectors at each of these conferences to hear
comments of the Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master and the Grand Secretary. All of these Grand Officers brought messages of great interest to the
Inspectors, and their remarks were always gratefully received.
I have this year attended schools in most of the Divisions, and I have observed
hand the efficient manner in which the Ritual is being communicated to the
first
at
Inspectors by our wonderful Assistant Grand Lecturers. It is a real pleasure to observe these experts in Masonic Ritual at work with their charges ... They are
each, truly skilled workmen of the very highest order, and it is through their efforts
that we are assured of continuing excellence of both Ritual and leadership.
On Friday, following the close of this Grand Lodge session, the Grand Lecturer's Annual School of instruction for the Inspectors will be held here in this
Auditorium.
In addition to all of the foregoing, regular schools of instruction have been
conducted in each of the Six divisions this year, and each of the 183 Inspectors
have held monthly schools within each District for the instruction of their individual Lodges and Brethren.

though we are speaking of a small percentage of the total, it should never the less
be of deep concern to us all, the fact that even a small number of our Lodges are experiencing such difficulties. In examining these problem areas, I .am more thoroughly convinced that their solution can be found only in more informed leadership at all levels of Lodge administration. We feel that this area has been to~ long
neglected and toward its resolution, the Committee on Ritual has re-doubled its e!forts to complete a comprehensive leadership program for use of ~he Lo?ges m
training Officers in all areas of Lodge administration previous to their election and
installation as key Officers in their individual Lodges.
At the risk of sounding like a broken record, I would again urge the Lodges to
dispense with the practice of requiring 8 or 9 years for an Officer to reac~ ~he
Master's chair. This practice acts as a deterrent to many excellently quahf1ed
Brothers who simply cannot commit such an extended period of time to going
through the chairs. We recommend that the progressive line of the Lodge
commence no lower than the Junior Deacon's Station, and that all offices below
that be filled strictly on a one year appointive basis. Many Brothers will volunte~r
to fill an officer's station if they were assured that it was for one year only. This
practice could greatly ease the problem of finding new Officer material, b~t it c~
be initiated only by the Lodges themselves. Again, we urge all Lodges to give senous consideration to such a change.
We must also re-emphasize the urgent need for more comprehensive programs of Masonic Education in the Lodges. It is in this area that we feel Masonry is
not fulfilling its obligation to the Candidate: Oh yes, we give him the three degrees
all right, but very little else: We are operating on the theory that Ritual alone makes
Masons. Well let me tell you, Brethren, nothing could be farther from the truth,
and the sooner we start educating our Candidates as well as raising them, then I
think we'll see Masonry begin to prosper.

Iii Honolulu we held an all day school for the Officers of all ten Hawaiian
J,.odges, Officers Coaches, Inspectors and all interested Masons of the area. The
Rinial of all three degrees was covered at this school and on the following day,
Sunday, another school was held for Candidates' Coaches. This school covered all
Candidates lectures. Both of these schools were excellently attended with Lodge
Officers flying in from all of the outer Islands to participate in, and study the Ritual. In Honolulu we were informed by Brother Alexander Bell of his intention to
retire from the lnspectorship of District 382. Our efforts fo find a qualified
replacement for Alex were unsuccessful. We therefore recommended to the Grand
Master that District 382 be temporarily dissolved. This recommendation was
implemented by the Grand Master. Kilauea Lodge was assigned to District 384 under Inspector Bill McKee, and Lodge Maui was assigned to District 385 under the
Inspectorship of Oswald Lau. This arrangement will continue until such time as a
fully qualified Past Master is available to serve as Inspector of District 382.
As regards the Inspectoral Corps in Hawaii, we received word in June that
Inspector John Pringle of District 385 could no longer continue his duties as
Inspector due to expanded work schedules.
On his visitation to Hawaii in July, the Grand Master conducted interviews,
selected and appointed Brother Oswald J.B. Lau to succeed Brother Pringle as
Inspector in District 385.
Masonry in Hawaii continues to prosper. This is not to say that the Hawaiian
Lodges are without problems, for in varying degrees, the same problems which
plague the Mainland Lodges are present in the Islands . Some of their problems,
both in Ritual and administration, were solved in our schools and discussions
while in the Islands. These visitations serve a very worthy purpose, for they give
our Hawaiian Brethren active assurance of the total and complete support of their
Brothers on the Mainland.
Mere word~ are insufficient to describe the depth of true Brotherly Love and
affection which is demonstrated in every Hawaiian Lodge, and by every member
thereof. Mark Twain described Hawaii as "the loveliest fleet of islands that lies
anchored in any ocean.'' This quotation is accurate but incomplete. To it should be
added "and manned by the most magnificent crew in God's Creation."
To those warm and wonderful Masons of Hawaii - Mahalo nui loa .

HAWAIIAN MASONRY

Immediately following the Division Three Conference in March this year, I
flew to Hawaii for the purpose of conducting Ritual schools, observing conditions
in the- Island Lodges, and searching out the solution to problems in certain areas of
Hawaiian Masonry.
On the Island of Hawaii I was met by Assistant Grand Lecturer, "Use" Patropulos and Officers of Kilauea Lodge. Schools and discussions were held in Hilo
before flying on to Maui, Kauai and Oahu.
On each Island, schools of instruction were held in the various degrees and
matters of Lodge administration were discussed.
On the Island of Kauai we were privileged to visit in, and inspect the new
Lodge room into which the Brethren of Kauai Lodge had moved in December,
1973. These new quarters are a definite improvement over their previous Lodge
hall. However, it was necessary for us to request that certain changes be made in
the Lodge room to provide for the proper reception of Candidates. The Master and
Brethren of Kauai Lodge were most cooperative in this matter and we are assured
that the prescribed changes have now been made.

1974-75 BUDGET
When our budget was submitted last year, we had no way of foretelling the
National financial crisis which has since rocked our Country's economy. Due to
some staggering increases in costs of food, lodging and travel, we have found it extremely difficult to hold the line on expenditures. We are proud to say however,
that due to restraint and good management on the part of the Inspectors and all
members of the Ritual Committee, we actually finished the year several dollars under our anticipated 1973-74 budget allowance.
We are constantly on the alert for new ways to trim costs without sacrificing
any of the services which this Committee renders, for instance, by moving the
Grand Lecturer's school to Friday following the Grand Lodge, the Inspectors do

92

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

not have to spend an extra two days in San Francisco as they have done in the past
because the school convened on Saturday before the Grand Lodge opening. This
change figures to save the Grand Lodge nearly $3000.00, and whercv~r possibl~,
like changes shall be effected to maintain our expenses at the lowest. figure ~ss1ble . We have submitted a budget request this year for $51,000.00. This fig_ure is actually lower than that of last year. We feel certain that with the co~perat1on of all
the Inspectors and members of this Committee, we shall be ab_le to d1schar~e ~II t~e
duties and responsibilities with which we are charged, and still operate within this
budgetary figure.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Trustees of Masonic Homes of California respectfully present their
Bighty-second Annual Report for the fiscal year June 30, 1974, with accompanying reports from the Administrators of the Home for the Aged at Union City
and of the Home for Children at Covina.
Masonic Homes of California is a charitable corporation, organized by Grand
[,odge under the laws of the State of California. Corporate powers are vested in the
Board of Trustees. As provided in the California Masonic Code, the Trustees are
twelve in number with the Deputy Grand Master, the Senior and Junior Grand
Wardens acting ex-officio, and nine members appointed by successive Grand
Masters.

ORGANIZATION

The Board of Trustees met in the California Masonic Memorial Temple, San
Francisco, immediately following the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
on October 12, 1973, for the purpose of Organization. The election of Burton
Meyer, Jr., Deputy Grand Master, John F. Roberts, Jr., Senior Grand Warden,
and Kermit A. Jacobson, Junior Grand Warden, was formally reported to the
Board. On motion duly made, seconded and carried they were confirmed as
Members of the Board.
Most Worshipful Raymond A. Ebbage, Grand Master, announced the
appointment of Jack H. Peloian, Charles Sedam and Myron E. Smith as Trustees,
each for three year terms. Their appointment was confirmed as Members of the
Board.
Due to the condition of his health Past Grand Master L. Harold Anderson,
who has served Masonry faithfully for many years and who had one year
remaining of his three year term, requested that he be relieved of his responsibility
as a Trustee. His request was reluctantly accepted, and Grand Master Ebbage
appointed Horace W. Orear, Jr., Past Master of California Lodge No. I, to serve
the balance of the unexpired term.
Because of the Board's desire to continue calling on Past Grand Master L.
Harold "Pete" Anderson for advice and assistance, they requested him to accept
an appointment as "Consulting Engineer." Brother Anderson has continued to
give of his time and talent this past year.
During the year the Board also lost the valuable services of Brother Ralph M.
Brown who, because of business and personal reasons, tendered his resignation as
a Trustee. The Grand Master appointed Brother Raymond A. Howe, a Past Master
of Palo Alto Lodge No. 346, to fill the vacancy.

REDEVELOPMENT AND REHABILITATION AT DECOTO

The Board of Trustees reported to Grand Lodge at the 1973 Communication
that, after careful study and evaluation of geological and seismic opinions and after
making long term projections of care and fmancial requirements,a Master Plan for
the redevelopment of the site was prepared in conjunction with the architects employed for the purpose.
As each of us is aware in reviewing ourown personal finances, this last year in
particular has seen the inflation of labor and material costs in tremendous
proportions. The months of January and February, 1974 alone, when extended to
an annual basis, reflect an increase in the cost of construction of twenty-five
percent. Moreover, the enactment of legislation affecting our proposed facility
added as much as five dollars per square foot to our projected building costs.
Your Trustees are charged with the responsibility of providing the finest available care for our residents within the means of the craft; and, simply stated, the
proposed Master Plan could not, as a result of these inflationary and legislative
influences, be carried into fruition within those means. The Redevelopment Committee returned again and again to the ''drawing board'' in an effort to provide a
desirable new development at Decoto and concluded in its recommendation,
adopted by the Board of Trustees, that a more modest program is required.
Several alternatives are available and are under continuing study. In the interim, since maintenance of substance has been deferred during the planning stages,
major steps have been taken to make needed repairs to, and renewal of, both the
physical home and the equipment. Plumbing and wiring are being renewed,
draperies and carpets are being installed and, generally, we are moving ahead as
rapidly as possible to provide an even more safe and comfortable Home in which
our guests may reside during their retirement years.
DECOTO OPERATIONS

Our residents at Decoto continue to enjoy the many activities and special
events at the Home as well as trips to surrounding areas, including ball games, the
theater, the Ice Follies, and other places of interest. We have at this time 375 guests
of whom 158 are in the nursing unit (Wollenberg Hall), 67 are considered semillllbulatory and 150 are ambulatory.

We announce, however, that although the Annual report by the Administrator
for the Masonic Home, Union City, which is submitted as a part of our report, has
been prepared by him, Hugh B. Herring, Administrator of our Home for the
elderly at Union City, after 12 years of devoted service submitted his resignation
from that responsibility for personal reasons effective September 22nd.
The Homes' Trustees accepted his resignation with expressions of
appreciation on behalf of the Board, the Fraternity, and the Residents of our Home
for his care and attention to the health and comfort of the guests.
To help maintain the continued care and comfort of the residents, J. Burton
Brown, Assistant Administrator of our Home for children at Covina, has been
appointed Interim Administrator at Union City until a replacement for Brother
Herring can be employed. In addition, former Administrator Brother Gail David
who at the time of his retirement had previously offered his services if ever needed,
is present as a volunteer during the period of transition on a consulting basis. Thus
the Home's opaations will continue smoothly and without interruption.
The Trustees are appreciative also of the dedication of the faithful employees
at both Homes and of their continuing desire to make each of them, not only a
comfortable place in which to live, but one in which the warmth oflove can be felt.
With the constancy of every member's support we will continue toward that end.

OUTSIDE REUEF
During recent years, we have seen a constant increase in the number of nonambulatory guests at Decoto and, to a lesser extent, an increase in ambulatory
guests as well. The non-ambulatory occupancy has now reached ~level wh~re it
will no longer be advisable to admit residents directly into those umts. W~.wish !O
emphasize, however, that those who are admitted in an ambulatory co?dition will
continue to receive all required care whether it be nursing home, hospital , or otherwise, as long as they are guests at the Home. Because of the high level of nonambulatory occupancy, therefore, it will be the policy of the Board of Trustees for
the foreseeable future, that no application for admission of one in a nonambulatory condition will be approved, except in the most extraordinary
circumstances.
Our non-ambulatory brethren, wives or widows are, of course, not abandoned
in a time of great need and it is the purpose of the Outside Relief program to provide this assistance. After all available assistance from family members who may
be legally required to contribute to support has been exhausted, and to the extent
other, private or public assistance is not available , monetary aid will be furn.ished
by the Masonic Homes usually in an amount not to excee~ t~e cost of c~e .m the
Home. It is anticipated that because of the policy of restnctmg the admission of
non-ambulatory residents, applications for Outside Relief will increase, and the
Homes office is prepared to assist the lodges as required in advising as to availability of other private and public sources, and in making application for assistance
by the Masonic Homes.
. .
Upon the recommendation of the Board of Trustees to equate th~~ receiv~g
the assistance of the brethren while living in the Home to those receiving Outside
Relief, the Grand Master directed the preparation of the nec~ssary documents
requiring recipients of Outside Relief to repay all amounts received to the extent
reasonably possible during life, and, in any event, upon death to the extent of all
assets in their estates:
It should be remembered that Outside Relief is intended only for long term
chronic needs and that temporary relief for specific purposes is to be cared for by
the individual lodges.

An outstanding Cornerstone and Dedication Ceremony was held August 18,
1973. Although it proved to be the hottest day of the year, we were privileged to
have most of our Grand Lodge Officers in attendance, as well as an estimated
2,000 brethren and wives, friends, and other civic dignitaries. The cornerstone
was made up of rocks indigenous to the areas in which our California Lodges are
located. The cornerstone elicited many favorable comments from the brethren at
the Ceremony, and others who have since visited us.

our medical needs. Its founder, Dr. W.P. Magan, started taking care of our children in the early l920's. Dr. Magan passed away this year.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:

Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board hereby submits its 42nd Annual Repart covering the fiscal year ending June 30, 1974.
INCOME FROM THE ENDOWMENT FuND

The Permanent Endowment Fund earned $1,536,853.10 this past year, which
amount has been transferred to the operating accounts of our two Masonic Homes.
Each year we realize how important this Endowment Fund is to the operation of
our Homes, without them an additional amount of $6. 97 from each member would
have been necessary.
BEQUESTS, GIFTS AND MEMORIALS

Bequests in the amount of $353,774.97 were received into the Endowment
Fund this past year. In addition, $1,332,486.84 was received by the Homes in
bequests from estates where the Endowment Fund was not specifically mentioned
in the will. Organizations and individuals made gifts in the amount of $5,553.81,
and memorials added $29 ,413 .16 to our funds. This makes a total of $1, 721,228. 78
received from bequests, individuals, organizations and memorials. It is important
to our Homes that we realize the value of bequests and wills, for it is the source of
substantial income.
INDIVIDUAL CONTRIBUTIONS
THROUGH LODGES

Each year •it has been possible to report increased contributions through
Lodges, and we are happy to be able to report that this year is no exception. Individual contributions through Lodges amounted to $1,039,246.43, another all time
high. The average amount per contributing member is $9. 53 as compared to $9 .08
last year. The percentage of participants was 49.50% and is a tribute to those
members who participated. We find, however, that we have yet to reach the other
so called 50% of our members who do not take the opportunity of contributing to
this most worthy cause.

RECOGJ\'ITION To LODGE SECRETARIES
We extend our special thank s to the Lodge Secretaries. It is through their efforts that our literature is mailed to the members, bringing our message to each
member of this Jurisdiction. They play a vital role in the success of our program
each year.
RECOGNITION FOR SPECIAL GIFTS
Each year we have Brethren who have given the Endowment Fund substantial
gifts to support the Homes, and we give them our sincere thanks. We would like to
encourage our members to consider this method of expressing their devotion to the
support of our Homes.

107

We believe every Brother is interested in knowing about the activities of our
Homes and the wonderful work Masonry is doing for our elderly at Decato and
children at Covina. We try to bring this information through the informative and
attractive I iterature that is available. This past year l ,356,000 pieces of literature
were distributed to our members and we feel this should encourage many of our
members to support this program. This material is on display in the exhibit area,
and we urge orders be placed at this Communication which will enable delivery to
be made within a few weeks.

SPECIAL CONSIDERAT!ONS
There is a great need for large sums to be used for the rehabilitation program at
Decato, and we urge our Brethren to give this their earnest consideration.
SERVICE ROLL CERTIFICATES
The new Service Roll Certificates which were distributed at the last Communication were well received and found to be real attractive. The tabs for those who
made the 1974 Service Roll will be sent to the Lodges for placement on the Certificates. The average contribution of three dollars per member is required for this
certificate.

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:

Your Board of Control has had the good fortune and great pleasure of serving
with the nineteen Masonic Service Bureaus in this great jurisdiction and who have
continued to contribute so much for relieving the distresses of Sojourners, their
widows and orphans while visiting or residing in the area served by the Bureaus.
This is the Forty-Seventh Annual Report of the Board of Control and covers
the fiscal year ending June 30, 1974. Copies of the minutes of our meetings were
sent to the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Senior and Junior Grand Wardens, Grand Secretary and the members of the Board of Control.
The Board of Control submitted all official actions, along with recommendations to the Grand Master for his approval, prior to placing them in effect. His
prompt action on these matters assisted the Board and the Bureaus materially and
to our Grand Master we are most appreciative.
Right Worshipful Kermit A. Jacobson, Junior Grand Warden, was appointed
as Liaison Officer to th~ Board of Control by the Grand Master, and was of most
1
valuable assistance.

138

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
MEETINGS

The Board held four business meetings during the year. One was held in
Northern California and one in Southern Califronia at which time the officers of
each Service Bureau in that area were invited to attend . During the meetings a twoway communication was encouraged. Informative and interesting presentations of
important subjects were presented by each member of the Board of Control.
Robert A. Klinger, a member of the staff of the Grand Secretary, was present and
told of the day-to-day activities of that office. Brother Klinger explained the preparation of tax reports for Lodges, and it is hoped that this service some day can be offered to the Secretaries of the Masonic Service Bureaus.
The two other meetings of the Board were held , one during the 1973 Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge, and the other in Southern California at which
time the budgets of our Bureaus were reviewed and approved.
It has been possible to reduce the number of meetings of the Board of Control
mainly due to the wonderful cooperation of the Bureaus in operating within the
Rules and Regulations. This reduction is reflected in the expenditures of the Board
of Control.
POLICY

At the request of the San Diego Masonic Service Bureau the Board reviewed,
sought the counsel of our Grand Secretary, and then recommended to the Bureaus
that the files of correspondence, records, and other material pertaining to the Service Bureau should be retained for a period of five (5) years and then destroyed if
the file space was required for other material. The only exceptions are: Minutes of
Meetings; the log record of Masonic Funerals; and Masonic Homes Investigations,
all of which are to be kept indefinitely.
Article XV, Section 6 of the Rules and Regulations for Operation of Masonic
Service Bureaus was amended to permit a Service Bureau not to be required to
secure their Annual Audit from aC.P.A. unless their budget exceeded $10,000.00.
The former amount was $7 ,500 .00. The Grand Master concurred in this recommendation and each Bureau was so notified.
TAXES

Continued attention has been given to the important preparation of both Federal and State tax forms and to assist each Bureau in problems which they have
encountered with their tax exempt applications, etc. The Board has continued to
work closely with the Chairman of the Taxation Committee, W. Stanley Davis,
through our Board Member Arthur R. Kirk . These dedicated Brothers have contributed countless hours of their time in these important matters, and we are most
grateful for this service and extend our sincere appreciation to each of them for
their attention to these problems .
UNIFORM COMPACTS

New compacts have been executed for these consolidated Lodges:
United Lodge No. 374
Wilshire-Garfield Lodge No. 445

AUDITS

Audits of the records and activities were made of the following Bureaus:
Bakersfield, Glendale, Fresno, Orange County, San Bernardino and Richmond.
CALIFORNIA FREEMASON

An article on the operations and functions of the Masonic Service Bureaus
was prepared by the Board and appeared in the Spring 197 4 issue of the California
Freemason. In addition there also appeared a listing of the Bureaus. The Board
appreciates the exposure to the members in this jurisdiction of this important Masonic service . It. is our hope that it has assisted our Brethren .
BUSH MASONIC RELIEF

The Board of Control pays special tribute to Ralph H. Head, the President of
the Bush Masonic Relief and to the Directors who serve with him, Most Worshipful Leo E. Anderson, P.G.M. and Louis Mahler. This Corporation provides funds
to pay for the operation of the six Masonic Service Bureaus in the Greater Los Angeles Area. The contributions they make to the Bureaus amounts to about
$60, 000. 00 each year. In addition, they contribute to other Masonic Chari ties. The
savings to the Lodges in the Bureaus in the Los Angeles area is material, and it is
hoped that the Masters of these Lodges will use these savings wisely for other Masonic Charities.
NEW EXECUTIVE SECRETARY

Stephen R. Millar was elected Executive Secretary of the Glendale Masonic
Service Bureau . He takes the place of Jordan P. Sims, who served faithfully in that
office since 1968.

REPORTS
All Bureaus submitted the required reports during the year, and they are in
summary form as appendages to this report. It is interesting that the total approved
budgets amounted to $100,463.00, which is a 16% increase over last year. Our
total operating expenses were $11,209 .00, which is a 3% increase over the
previous year. Within this amount is $6,075.00 for State and Federal Taxes. Our
Bureaus conducted 803 Funerals for Sojourner Master Masons, and made over 993
calls on sick brothers, conducted 484 investigations, and assisted in preparing 57
applications to Masonic Homes.
.
The Board of Control expresses appreciation to all the Executive Secretaries,
the Presidents of the Bureaus as well as the Officers and Committeemen who served the nineteen Bureaus for their dedicated work during the past year. Special
appreciation is extended to the Grand Master, the Grand Secretary and his Staff,
and to the Chairman of the Taxation Committee.
The Board of Control has functioned well within their budget this past year
and herewith requests the sum of $1,250.00 to cover expenses during the ensuing
year. This is a reduction of $750.00 from the present budget.

CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple herewith
submits its Twentieth Annual Report.
The terms of the appointive Trustees of the Board of Trustees are, as follows:

At the close of the 1973 Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, the Board
of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple held its Annual Meeting.
The Board of Trustees then proceeded to nominate and elect the following officers
to serve for the ensuing year until new ones are elected.
DeWald M. Baum ...................................... President
Ira W. Coburn, P.G.M ............................... Vice-President
Chester R. MacPhee, P.G.M .............................. Treasurer
Edward H. Siems, P.G.M ................................. Secretary
Burton Meyer, Jr. ............................. Deputy Grand Master
This year our Masonic Memorial Temple celebrated its sixteenth birthday. At
each Annual Communication many members of the Fraternity who were not
Master Masons at the time of its dedication, attend Grand Lodge for the first time.
We believe that it is appropriate to remind them that this magnificent building is
our first Grand Lodge Temple, conceived and built by the Craft as its permanent
headquarters. Its conception and birth required eleven years filled with vision,
frustration and finally achievement. It can be truly said that when our Brethren
built a building of their own, they did so in magnificent style. Not for nothing are
we as Masons called builders. We truly practice what we preach.
Our California Masonic Memorial Temple, located at the top of prestigious
Nob Hill, has each year added to its reputation as an outstanding complex for the
cultural, civic and educational activities of this great metropolitan city. Here are
presented to all our very substantial contribution to the beautification of San
Francisco and the advancement of civilization in general. May the Great Architect
of the Universe grant that this building will always shine as a beacon light of our
Fraternity's determination to always support and advance a free public school system for the education of the generations of Americans yet to be.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

147

Acoustically, it has no peer for concerts, stimulating lectures and the
performance of musical and dramatic presentations. It furnishes an outstanding
setting for the dramatic exhibitions of the new creations of industry and the fine
arts. Business organizations, fraternal, state governmental departments and
professional associations are continually increasing their use of our facilities for
their meetings. It is an excellent showcase for their numerous activities.
TOURS AND VISIT ATIO NS

The Temple is open daily, except Saturday and Sunday, for visitors from 8:45
a.m. to 4:45 p.m. If there are other activities in the Temple on Saturday or Sunday
then additional tours are arranged. We have had guests from every one of the
States and from many of the countries of the world visiting our Temple. This year
we were hosts to visitors from the following countries:
Australia
Austria
Canada
England
France
Germany

Iran

Taiwan
Turkey
Members of the craft from the 50 States and from many foreign countries
request information to take home to their respective lodges. They are amazed at the
beauty of our Temple. We learn continually that we are a unique Grand
Jurisdiction and in the forefront of the activities of Freemasonry.
Many representatives of Senior Citizen groups, Rainbow for Girls, Job's
Daughters, DeMolay Chapters and other concordant bodies continue to arrange for
tours of our beautiful building. Hundreds of public school children visit our
Te~ple an~ it mak~s a lasting impression on them of our efforts to help them
achieve their potential of a better life through free public school education.

MAINTENANCE AND IMPROVEMENTS

Nothing less than the highest stanqards of maintenance will continue to prese!"e the classic beauty of our Temple. After 16 years of use and occupancy, certain of .the. mechanical equipment of necessity will require replacement or
modernization. The elevators needed further dock and directional controls the hot
water boiler tubes of necessity required repairs and replacement, the Pin~ Street
ramp w~s renovated to prote~t the metal panel. All portions of the building not
faced with marble must be painted and the exterior marble facing must be cleaned
after so many years of use to remove the embedded grime to prevent deterioration
?fthe surface. The painting and marble will not be done until the apartment building being built next door is ready for occupancy. We have been informed that the
c.ompletion d~te is this year. The interior painting, stripping and waxing is a continual necessity to not only preserve the charm and usefulness of our building but
also the surface from erosion through wear and tear. Most of this interior main-

PuBLIC RELATIONS AND CIVIC AFFAIRS

0cCUPANCY

Membership in the Nob Hill Association, San Francisco Convention _and
Visitors Bureau, the Press Club of San Francisco and the Greater San Francisco
Chamber of Commerce serves us as a much needed contact with prominent civic
and business leaders from whom many rental prospects and much useful information of value can be obtained.
Our staff has been instructed and is making every effort to give that extra
excellence in service and attention to our tenants that results in repeated use of our
facilities. Their fine cooperation does not only build a better image of our
Fraternity but also makes the use of our fine facilities more enjoyable for our
tenants and increases their desire for further use . Numerous tenants have
commented most favorably in letters to us of this unusual attention to their anticipated needs.

During the past year our Auditorium, because of its excellent accoustical properties, has been used for some of the finest concert and theatrical-type of
performances. This has enhanced the fine reputation of the Temple as a place of
culture and refinement befitting the admirable image of California Freemasonry.
Your Trustees believe this type of use of our premises should be continually
encouraged.
A number of new hotels and additions with the most modem of convention facilities have been completed in the past year. We have to be cognizant that each
new facility is and will be competitive for our rental clientele insofar as meeting
.
space, Exhibition Hall and Auditorium use is concerned.•
With this in mind, your Trustees believe it is most desirable that the present policy of diversified rental of the Auditorium and Exhibition Hall be followed as a
protection against the lessening use of either one by the booking of only one form
of tenancy. Each new hotel will encourage and should bring some additional convention business to San Francisco and increase its reputation as an ideal place to
hold meetings.
Our Auditorium is well adapted to all kinds of stockholder and business meetings. Space does not permit a full recital of the many corporations and groups that
have used the Auditorium and the Exhibition Hall for important meetings.
It is most gratifying that well known educational institutions have held their
graduation exercises in our facility because of its beauty and impressive dignity
that the setting contributes to the historic occasion.

We will miss them.

mailed to every Grand Jurisdiction in the United States and to others m the free

Referred to Committee on Finance (Budget allocation)

The Committee on Finance:
The recommendation of the California Freemason Publication Board that the
per capita tax for the California Freemason Magazine be increased from 35 cents to
40 cents has been referred to the Committee on Finance. The present per capita of
35 cents has remained unchanged for the past eight years . While this assessment
proved adequate to cover publication expenses for the early years of this period,
during the past four years a deficit of over $22,000 has accumulated, and for the
current year an additional $13 ,000 deficit is projected.
In the belief that each function or activity of Grand Lodge should, insofar as possible, be self supporting, we concur that the per capita be increased to 40 cents for
t?e current year. There is every reason to believe that publication costs will contmue to escalate and that further increases may be necessary in future years.
Adopted.
