REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:
For the third successive year there have been no Lodges instituted and so your
Committee on Charters has no Lodges under Dispensation upon which to report.
We again deplore this situation. We recognize that older cities may have no need
of additional Lodges and may even need to consolidate existing Lodges, but the
other side of the coin is that new suburban communities are being formed that
have no Masonic organizations of any kind. In his fine report yesterday our
Grand Master pointed out that younger men are again taking an interest in Masonry. Most of the younger families live in these new communities and it is a
challenge to our Fraternity to provide the Lodges and Masonic organizations for
the entire families .
It is not the function of the Committee on Charters to go into these new areas
to recruit members to start Lodges. The initial spark must come from those who
will start the Lodge - but once the spark is struck, we stand ready to assist and
advise. There is also a manual available from Grand Lodge which details the
steps necessary in forming a Lodge. I sincerely urge any of you who live near
such communities to accept this challenge and find other Masons to join with you
in starting Lodges. You will find it one of the most rewarding projects in which
you have ever taken part.
There has been referred to our Committee that portion of the report of the
Grand Secretary listing changes of meeting place of several Lodges and also that
portion dealing with Charter Amendments. Sixteen Lodges consolidated:
Sunset Lodge No. 352 and Albert Pike Lodge No. 484, effective December 4,
1973, to be known as Sunset Lodge No. 352.

Respectfully submitted,
KENNETH HEMPHILL, Chairman

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
FOR FISCAL YEAR ENDING JUNE 30, 1974
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F . & A. M. of California:
The past year has been a difficult one in the investment market with both bond
and stock prices declining in the face of extremely high interest rates, continuing
inflation, political turmoil and international monetary problems created by the vast
flow of funds to the oil producing nations, largely representing outflows from the
United States and other industrialized nations. Accordingly, the total market value
of the investment portfolio under our control declined to $37 ,618,218 at June 30,
1974, as compared with a total of $40,518 ,869 at the end of the prior year. In spite
of the decline in market value, the estimated annual income has increased from
$2,217 ,988 to $2,455,470, a gain of 10.7%.
Activites of the Committee are regulated by the Masonic Code, which sets forth
the three major categories (as groups) of securities allowable for investment.
These categories are summarized as follows:
(1) Group I - Consists of cash, savings accounts, obligations of the United
States, obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions, and such
other securities as are legal for savings banks in California and Hawaii. In general.
Group I may be said to consist of the highest grade and most conservative

156

157

PROCEEDINGS OF TIIE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

securities. At least 20% of the funds available for investment must be maintained
in such securities.
(2) Group II - Consists generally of bonds, debentures, and other evi~ences
of indebtedness which do not meet the qualifications of Group I. It also consists of
preferred stocks which are listed on a National Securities Exchange and the preferred stocks of corporations whose common stocks are eligible for investment in
Group III.
.
.
(3) Group III - Consists of common stocks, which must be fully hsted and
registered on a national exchange registered with the Securities and Exhcnage
Commission, bank and insurance company stocks, shares of investment trusts,
and savings accounts with savings and loan associations. Total inv~stments in
Group III securities are generally limited to 60% of the total portfoho.

at market values, compared with the portfolio as of a year earlier:

Convertible issues make up 16.44% of the portfolio and are represented by
debentures and preferred stocks which yield 7.6% at market and are convertible
into the common stock of the issues held. This type of investment provides good
current income while also having the potential for capital appreciation in a more fa.
vorable stock market climate.
Common stocks represent over 50% of the Fund and, in our opinion, continue
to be appropriate considering the investment objectives. While the market value of
the common stocks decreased 16.03% over the past year, this compares very fa.
vorably with most common stock indexes and with publicly reporting mutual
funds.
Our investment strategy continues to stress quality, balance and patience.
Quality will be a particularly important criterion over the coming years. We define
corporate quality in terms of outstanding management, strong finances, dominant
or unique competitive position, excellent products and services and above average
growth prospects. To the extent that companies possess these qualities, they
should be able to lead and/or benefit from significant changes, maintain or increase
market share, and retain or improve profitability.
Portfolio balance, which is also an important measure of flexibility, is likely to
be another essential element of investment success . A compelling reason for balance in current investment strategy is the growing probability that the domestic
economy recovery in 1975 will be more balanced than normal. Public spending
(private investment) will be stronger than usual in the next economic upswing and
consumer spending will be more restrained because of continuing pressures on real
disposable income. The balanced portfolio both from the standpoint of fixed income versus equities and a proper sector weighting within the equity portion
should perform best in a balanced recovery.
And finally, tl\e concept of patience is a very essential ingredient in a successful
investment strategy. There is a distinct difference between investment patience
and complacency. Investment complacency implies doing nothing for the sake of
decision; investment patience connotes the inner confidence and courage to take
appropriate portfolio actions and to wait for superior value and selectivity to prevail in the market.
Respectfully submitted,
JACK F. BOWLEY, Chairman

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Your Committee on Commercialism herewith submits its report for the year
just ending.
Infractions of our laws, rules and regulations under the jurisdiction of this committee have been minor in nature. No Masonic trial resulted from any matter of
violation.
The infractions or violations have been handled through discussion and an understanding. Those in violation have agreed to cease and desist. Several examples
of items referred to the Commercialism Committee are as follows :
A Company, which sells a food product to organizations for fund raising
projects, recently sent letters to several of our Masonicly associated youth groups,
offering their product to those who might be interested. The letter was signed by
the President of the company, who also added his title of Past Master and listed his
Lodge name and number under his signature. After a discu~sion wit~ on~ of our
Committee Members , the Brother agreed that the use of his Masonic Title and
Lodge affiliation was not only a violation of the advertising section of the Masonic
Code, but was in poor taste, and he agreed not to use his title and Lodge name
again. The poetic justice of this case was , that the company did not make even one
sale from the distribution of this letter.
The square and compass is registered with the California Secretary of State as
the official insignia of the Grand Lodge of California, and its use is regulated by
the California Masonic Code and any individual wishing to use that insignia must
first obtain permission to do so from the Grand Master. Over the years, the_square
and compass has been used by individual Masons on business cards, stationary,
and in their advertising, but when approached by a committee member with the explanation of the Code violation, our members have agreed to cease and desist.
A new use of the insignia has cropped up this year on personal checks. After
discussions with several Banks, it was found that the check printing catalogs of
most all banks in California and Hawaii, offer hundreds of personalized monograms which can be printed on personal checks for their customers. Three cases
have been brought to the attention of the committee in the past few months and after a consultation with one of our committee members, the Brothers have agreed to
discontinue the use of the checks and have new ones printed. As a word of caution
to all Master Masons, if a personal check is noticed with the square and compass
printed on it, whisper good counsel in the Brother's ear.
The Committee met on April 6, 1974 for the purpose of drafting a Manual on
Commercialism. After a lengthy debate on the various aspects of such a Manual, it
was finally determined that one Manual would be unsatisfactory for the various
bodies that must conform to its policies. It is presently contemplated that three (3)
sections to the Manual will be proposed for adoption. The first section will be directed to the conduct of Lodge affairs and that of Master Masons living within the
jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California. The

REPORT OF CODE COMMISSION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
The primary responsibility of the Code Commission is to prepare the pocket
supplement to the California Masonic Code each year . This work is done during
and shortly after the Annual Communication. Your Commission prepared and,
with the assistance of the Grand Secretary's Office, had published the supplement
following the 1973 Annual Communication . This required codifying the various
amendments, additions, and deletions to the Constitution and Regulations as well
as the selection and preparation of annotations from the Grand Master's Decisions,
the Grievance Committee report, and the reports of other Grand Lodge Boards and
Committees. The Code Commission will work at the 1974 Annual Communication to prepare the next supplement.
It is anticipated that the new revision of the California Masonic Code will be
published shortly and that this will necessitate one or two meetings of the Code
Commission in order to resolve the minor problems that inevitably arise with a new
revision. We would therefore request that our budget be increased to $1650.00 to
cover any necessary expenses .

IDAHO

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Most Worshipful Grand Master, delegates, and distinguished guests , the
California Correspondence Committee, in addition to the Articles which are published from time to time in the California Freemason, submits an Annual Report to
the Grand Master for his consideration at the Annual Communication of the Fiscal
Year of his term as Grand Master.
The rights of conscience, the equality of all men before the Law, the separation
of Church and State, religious toleration, freedom of speech and of the press, public schools, are vital traditions of the American people. They are not brought in
question; they form the stock of firm and universal convictions on which our national life is based; they are ingrained into the character of our people and you can
assume, in any controversy, that an American will admit their truth . .. They are
never explicitly taught to us, but we assimulate them in our earliest childhood from
all our surroundings at the fireside, at school, from the press, on the highways and
streets . We never hear them disputed by the great majority of Americans. The fight
for Liberty and Rights can never let up. It is as right to stand firm forour Rights as it
is to do our duties. As men are made, Liberty and Rights do not descend from
heaven in a gentle shower, but have to be won and defended, day by day; but always under the Rules or Laws. As Masons we accept the foregoing principles
without question, knowing full well that as Masons we try to apply them in our
every day living to the end that as individuals we as well as our fellow man are
better qualified to carry on the traditions of Free Masonry.
Time does not permit references to every Grand. Lodge Jurisdiction, and accordingly our references for the most part will be brief and concise.
COLORADO

The Grand Master of Colorado does not agree with those who say that our prestige has fallen . It is his opinion that the Masonic prestige is as high , or higher than it
ever might have been, because that prestige is, and always has been based upon the
community acceptance of our activities and programs and upon morality and upon
rightness displayed by each individual Mason in our community.
CONNECTICUT

The Grand Master's program on Grand Master's day was called "Accent on
Youth" and featured singing groups , clowns and musicians from its Masonic
Youth groups.

The Grand Lecturer pointed out that to read the names affixed to the Declaration
of Independence is almost to call the roll of distinguished Masons of that time. Traditions say that Masons had an important part in the Boston Tea Party. George
Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Franklin, and John Hancock, to name a
few , were the authors of our heritage. It is to them that our debt of obligation to
carry on as free men under a constitutional government must be paid.
INDIANA

The Grand Master had much to say about the size of Lodges, except for the obvious economic factor. To all intents and purposes any membership of a large
Lodge over and above 315 members is of little value to the Lodge. Many Brethern
live far away, and of course can never attend, but the fact remains that although the
great rank and file could attend, they do not.

.

KANSAS

Ever since 1717, when the Grand Lodge of England was formed and began to
teach responsibility to responsible men, to be concerned with freedom and the
welfare of their Brethern, widows and orphans, Freemasonry has subscribed to the
Brotherhood of Man under the Fatherhood of God. There are over 26 Grand
Lodges in the ·united States which operate homes like the Grand Lodge of
California. Others engage in other forms of care for aged Brethern, widows and
orphans. Altogether a reliable estimate of the total amount of funds expended by
various Masonic agencies, Grand Lodges and affiliated groups currently aggregate
more than $35,000,000.00 per year. Crippled children hospitals operated by the
Nobles of the Mystic Shrine account for a considerable portion of this amazing total which is augmented by funds such as that of California. Under our Masonic obligations, we believe we are committed to the care of the unfortunate. Charity is
one of our fundamental obligations . Jn short we are our Brother's Keeper .
LOUISIANA

In our time,, a most important era in the history of man , the principles of
Freemasonry take on an additional significance. It is entirely possible that
Freemasonry, which played a primary role in the establishment of our Republic,
must eventually save it. We should rededicate ourselves to these principles.
MAINE

There are two problems, that are still problems in Lodges of Maine; namely
smoking in the Lodge halls before and after meetings, and the use of alcoholic beverages in Masonic Temples.

MARYLAND

KNIGHTS OF COLUMBUS

On September I Ith, 1973, the Grand Master granted a dispensation to
Amicable Lodge No. 25 to hold its regular meeting on board of the U.S. Frigate
Constellation. 175 years before, Amicable Lodge No. 25 had been granted its
charter by the Grand Lodge of Maryland. The City of Maryland was incorporated
and the ''Constellation'' our Nation ' s First Warship, was launched at Harris Creek
in Baltimore.

California Freemasonry has never been in controversy with the Roman Catholic
Church, nor has our craft taken official recognition of any of the pronouncements
against it by any church or anyone else. In recent years, both in Indiana and in other
parts of the nation, there has been a relaxing of the Roman Church's restraint, and a
ripening friendship between Masonry and the Knights of Columbus. Masonic
Lodges have entertained Knights of Columbus and their ladies . Knights of Columbus and their ladies have reciprocated and in many instances have been the ones
to make the first gesture of friendship. There are many similarities between the two
organizations: in our system of three degrees; in our efforts to help, aid, and assist
our less fortunate members; in our aims to improve the community through the
improvement of the individual member; in our active sponsorship of well rounded
and wholesome activities for the youth who come under the sphere of the
respective organizations.
The official publication of the Indiana Grand Lodge, "The Indiana
Freemason," has on occasion published articles written by ladies and spokesmen
of the Roman Catholic church and the Knights of Columbus . These articles .in
"The Indiana Freemason" have not only been complimentary to Freemasonry,
but have expressed pleasure at the bridge of friendship that is being built so carefully between the Grand Lodge of Indiana and the Knights of Columbus.

MISSISSIPPI

This Grand Lodge with the assistance of the local Lodges pays out between
$30,000.00 and $40,000.00 each year to the distressed Masons, their widows and
orphans.
MONTANA

This Jurisdiction has successfully tried to bring something of value to each
member and each Lodge.
NEBRASKA

Masons are taught to be good Citizens of the Country of which they are a part,
and it behooves our American Masons to pay particular interest at this time to good
government in our Country; taking a firm stand for the public schools as the first
defense against the divisiveness which periodically threatens our American Way
of Life.
NEW HAMPSHIRE

This Jurisdiction currently has two outstanding projects; the first is the publication of a new book entitled ''Three centuries of Freemasonry in New Hampshire.''
The second has been the Grand Lodge Masonic Homes Improvement Fund Drive.
OHIO

This Jurisdiction for 10 years has been engaged in an educational program, during which it has granted $400.00 cash to each of26 students in Ohio Colleges and
seminaries. Feeling that educational institutions are better qualified than the Committee of Ohio Grand Lodge to select deserving scholars, the awarding of the
scholarship has always been left entirely to the discretion of the scholarship boards
of the collegiate associations.
OKLAHOMA

In 1962 it was suggested by an Oklahoma Mason, that the Masonic Education
Committee should sponsor Masonic roadside signs, so that Masons traveling
through the state might know that a Masonic Lodge was in town and its location,
also the night on which it held its meetings . The program proved to be very successful, and Oklahoma now has Masonic Lodge signs throughout the State.

OREGON

The Masonic and Eastern Star Home of Oregon, Forest Grove, Oregon, established 1922 admits adults only . The Home is operated jointly by the Grand Lodge
of Oregon and the Grand Chapter, O.E.S. of Oregon. Master Masons, their wives
and/or widows and members of the Order of Eastern Star are accepted, provided
they have been members in good standing for ten years prior to their applications.
PENNSYLVANIA

The Masonic Homes of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, Elizabethtown,
Pennsylvania, established in 1913, admits adults and children . This large home is
located on a 15,000 acre parcel of land. A major commercial farm is conducted
there by the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania.

matter thereof would be cumulative, often repetitive. The Committee respectfully
submits this within report and requests that it be filed, and that the report insofar as
it requests for the next fiscal year a budget of $400.00, be referred to the Finance
Committee.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
I
BRAZIL

Those who follow the report of this Committee will be aware of our general policy with respect to Brazilian Freemasonry. There are twenty-one State Grand
Lodges, of which eighteen have, over the years, sought fraternal relations with the
Grand Lodge of California. Investigations having proven that our tests for
recognition were met, all eighteen have been recognired by this Grand Lodge. No
such requests have been received from the three other State Grand Lodges, one of
whom, the Grand Loja do Estado do Acre, was recently established on August 20,
1973 through a charter issued by the Grand Loja do Amazonas e Territorios
Limitrofas seated at Manaus, which ceded the State of Acre to the new Grand
Lodge.
The correctness of our attitude towards the Grand Orient of Brazil has been
substantiated by a circular letter received July 9, 1974 from Brother Kurt Max
Hauser, Grand Secretary of Foreign Relations of the Grand Loja do Rio Grande do
Sul, who is an outstanding authority on Freemasonry in South America. Briefly
stated, it appears that last year a number of subordinate State Grand Lodges dissolved their ties with the Grand Orient of Brazil. The State Grand Lodges hoped
that this might be a settlement leading to some reunification but unhappily this has
not proved to be the case. Incidentally, Brother Hauser states unequivocably that

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:
Again we have passed another milestone in our young history. Our Constitution
is 187 years old this past month and, in spite of all the trials and tribulations as to
what our forefathers meant in its language and which body of government answers
to which other bodies, we are still the United States of America. History is replete
with forms of government that were truly great, even world conquerors, that
crumbled because of lesser things than have happened to our government. Our
Constitution may have its weaknesses and certainly a flaw here and there but
nowhere on this earth is there to be found a better one.
Our Grand Master, who served so many years on this very same Committee, set
the tone of this year's events when he stated he wanted all Masons to strive to pass
the word, "THE CONSTITUTION IS FOR EVERYONE - LET'S GET INVOLVED." We have endeavored through the lnspectoral corp to have all Lodges
use their Lodge Manual which contains suggested guidelines on staging a successful Constitution Observance Program . We made available , for the first time , posters as well as pamphlets to be distributed at gatherings for the general public.
In reading and rereading the reports of Chairmen for the past decade, it is very
evident that we are faced with the same problems today that perhaps the framers of
our Constitution were confronted with. We talk today of lack of interest in any
given project, particularly if it is to arouse the public interest. So how do we
promote an intangible item that cannot be felt, seen, heard or bought at the local
discount store. We , as Masons , think we have the answer - tell as many other
people as possible, regardless of race, creed or sex, about this great document that
gives us all the basic freedoms that, to this very day, people are fighting wars to obtain. Again we ask, what were the thoughts of these men who wrote this great document? Were they , too , fighting for an aroused public for support? You can rest
assured they were!
In our year of 1974 then, we have set the theme for the big year to come. We
will shortly be celebrating our 200th anniversary and with this thought in mind, we
have strived to get as many as possible of our Brethren involved. Ifwe were only to

Following is the combined report of the Committee on Masonic Information
and Responsibility and its Subcommittees.
LODGE INFORMATION PROORAMS :

I) Masonic Workshops: We are continuing to assist the Lodges, and in some
cases groups of Lodges, in sponsoring workshops in areas of Masonic Education
other than Ritual. Activity this past year has necessitated considerable work in restaffing the Committee to better serve the entire jurisdiction. Workshops have
been held in cooperation with the Lodge Officers to promote and enhance the interest of the general membership in Freemasonry.

Committee has been reviewing all research Lodge material intended for publication, reviewing all correspondence contemplated with other Grand Jurisdictions

David C. Lee. Generally speaking it is an editing assignment and one of constructive assistance. Occasionally a Jack of communication has presented
problems, but thus far it has always been possible to settle such problems with direct discussion and mutual understanding.

Lodges, Service Clubs and School Groups. This has been accomplished by a dedicated group of Masons only indirectly related to the Committee under the
Chairmanship of C. Clifford Geddes. These programs have been presented primarily in the Sacramento Valley and Mother Lode areas.

Rush, Jr., this work consists of a continuing correspondence and a close working
relationship with designated members of other Grand Jurisdictions. When the
Grand Lodge of California originates new material or when other Grand Lodges do
so, much information is mutually exchanged on various projects and their effects
on our respective memberships. Such material, when requested, is obtained for
one of the Grand Lodge Committees or for one of the Grand Lodge Officers and is
usually thereafter presented to the Grand Lodge Library for future reference and
study by those who might be interested.

This is shown by many letters of appreciation from students who have received
our grants, and we always have a back-log of approximately 100 applications waiting to be processed by our Scholarship Committee.
As will be seen from the above list of donees, however, our charitable donations for purposes other than scholarships have been significant. The $5,000.00 to

will see your presentation bring great benefits for humanity.''
The cleft palate program was adopted during the past year to assist Stanford
University Hospital in its program of research and care and treatment of children
who have been born with birth defects relating particularly to the palate. The
Doctors at Stanford University Hospital are pioneers in this field and the results
achieved there have been almost miraculous.
In conclusion, it can be seen that substantial progress toward fulfillment of the
goal of assisting and benefitting all mankind as provided in our By-Laws, has been
made. Admittedly, there is still much to do, but it is anticipated that during the next
fiscal year, throogh the dedicated work of our Board members, whose names appear hereafter, we shall make even greater progress.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Again it becomes my pleasant duty to report to the Officers and members of this
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge on the California Masonic Foundation, its
purposes, objectives, and plans for the future.
The governing body of the Foundation is a Board of Trustees, consisting of
fifteen (15) members, all of whom are required by our By-Laws and Articles oflncorporation to be members of Grand Lodge. The Officers are elected annually and
consist of a President, a Vice-President, a Secretary and an Assistant Secretary, a
Treasurer and an Assistant Treasurer. The Grand Secretary is also our Secretary
and the Grand Treasurer is our Treasurer.
Our assets consist of cash, notes secured by Trust Deeds, and investments in
bonds and stocks, all of which totalled as at the close of the fiscal year, June 30,
1974, approximately $1,089,000.00. Full accounting records are kept and maintained in the Grand Secretary's office and are open for inspection.
Total income last year was approximately $74,000.00, all of which was used for
charitable purposes, except such as was needed to defray necessary expenses for
accounting, stationery and supplies, printing and mailing, investment counsel,
and travel expenses of Trustees for attending meetings.
Charitable purposes undertaken during the year were as follows:
Educational grants
DeMolay Leadership Training
Cleft Palate Program at Stanford University Hospital
Grant to Masonic Homes for new construction program
California Scottish Rite Foundation to be used particularly for its
aphasia program

Our scholarship program has, in our opinion, proven very successful. To
qualify, a student must send our Scholarship Committee a formal application, the
form of which will be supplied on request, containing information as to his grades,
his course of study, his financial need, where he wishes to go to school, etc.
Many of the students are recommended through local Lodges, in which case, if
the applicant qualifies and the grant is approved, an award ceremony is held at the
recommending Lodge to which the student's parents and relatives are invited, and
the check is presented by the Master or Inspector of the Lodge. Male and female
applicants are equally eligible.
The average award for one school year is $500. 00, but the student may be granted a similar award in a subsequent year. Often these amounts, although seemingly
small, are sufficient when added to the student's other available funds, to make the
difference in whether he can or cannot get an education.

REPORT OF DE MOLAY LIAISON BOARD

AFTERNOON SESSION -Tuesday , October 15, 1974

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

This Board, established by Most Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner at the time
that he was Grand Master, is the vehicle by which the Grand Master is infonned of
DeMolay activities . It operates only on the executive level through the Executive
Officer of the Jurisdiction of Southern California, Melvin A. Pixley, the Executive
Officer of the Jurisdiction of Northern California, John L. Wixon, and the Executive Officer of the Jurisdiction of Hawaii, Clifford H. Hinton of the Order of
DeMolay. On national matters it operates through the International Supreme
Council Order of DeMolay at Kansas City.
The DeMolay Liaison Board acts best when it has nothing to do. Such has been
the case during the past Masonic year, as there were no DeMolay problems to be
solved which would require the action of the Grand Master. Such contacts with Executive Officers and Committee Members as were necessary were by correspondence, face-to-face communication, or by telephone; consequently, no expenditures were made by the Committee this year. It is requested, however, that
$500.00 be budgeted for the coming year in the event that meetings of the Board
become necessary.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Lodge Financing hereby submits its report concerning the
activities of that committee during the past Masonic year. Apparently, as a result
of the c~rren! status of the economy and the unusually high interest rates, the committee fmds itself to be somewhat less active than in prior years. It is to be noted
that the majority of the applications received by the committee concern repairs, alterations or modifications to existing Masonic Temples with a substantial decrease
in the number of new Temples being constructed and a like decrease in the number
of purchases of future Temple sites. Information concerning the specific
applications and the actions taken therein including actions taken at the annual
communications will be found in detail on the pages following this report and will
be included in the published proceedings .
The range of activities has again been varied covering applications to transfer
funds from the general funds of the Lodge to a Temple Association in return for either promissory notes or membership certificates in said association; applications
for expenditures for repairs and modification s of various types , i.e . air
conditioning, kitchens, dining rooms, etc .; applications for the purchase of vacant
properties and .improved properties; applications for approval of new Masonic
Te~ple. Associations and for reorganized Masonic Temple Associations ;
apphcatlons for approval of new loans or refinancing as well as applications for
approval of various long term leases.
In addition to the applications, which have been acted upon, many other
miscellaneous inquiries have been directed to members of the committee and we
have attempted to be of service to the brethren.
Numerous visitations were made by members of the committee to various
Lod~es, at their request, to advise and counsel with the brethren concerning
particular problems respecting Lodge and Temple Association matters. Your committee is always most happy to serve in this way and it is anticipated that in the
ensuing year many more such visitations will be made.
The various financial reports, as submitted by the Temple Association in accordance with Section 200 of the California Masonic Code, have also been forwarded to the committee and reviewed by them. These reports indicate the serious
problems that many Temple Associations are having in meeting their expenses,
particularly in the area of real property taxes . On the encouraging side the reports
d? ~ndicate a continued trend toward the establishment of a reserve for depreciation. It should become increasingly aware, however, that in today's rising economy the burden of maintaining Masonic Temples will continue to grow as the

To theMost Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Pay of Members submits the following report covering the
125th Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
Those entitled to mileage compensation are the Master, or in his absence, the
ranking Warden, or in the absence of the Master and Wardens, the duly Elected
Representative and Past Grand Masters, if they attend Grand Lodge in such capacity only. However, when a Master and Warden from the same Lodge are present at
an Annual Communication, and one of said Officers serves on a Grand Lodge
Committee entitled to travel and expense reimbursement, he shall be reimbursed
accordingly; the other Officer shall receive reimbursement under Section 174,
California Masonic Code, as the Officer representing his Lodge on the floor of
Grand Lodge.
Mileage from the various points within the State of California to San Francisco
has been taken from the published records of the California State Automobile
Association. Mileage from points in the State of Hawaii to San Francisco has been
taken from the published reports of air lines, in accordance with Sections 174 and
176, California Masonic Code. No compensation is allowed to members from San
Francisco or the immediate vicinity. Compensation of members from the State of
California has been computed on the basis of ten ( 10) cents per mile, the rate fixed
by the Committee on Finance. Compensation of the members from the State of
Hawaii has been figured on the basis of published first class round-trip air rates of
regularly scheduled major air lines, from Honolulu to San Francisco, plus interisland air fare to Honolulu, when necessary.
The payroll has been checked with the registration records as submitted to us by
the Committee on Credentials, and the amounts required to meet the transportation
costs for the 1974 Annual Communication are as follows:
Past Grand Masters (not on Committees) .................... $ None
Representatives of Lodges .................. : ......... $ 35,310.23
Total ....................................... $ 35,310.23
Checks will be ready for distribution at the Registration Desk on Thursday
morning immediately following the election of the Junior Grand Warden.
Brethren, if you are the Master or Warden representing your Lodge, or the duly
Elected Representative of your Lodge, the Pay of Members Committee urgently
requests you to promptly pickup your check.
Arrangements have been made so that those who wish to cash their checks may
do so at the United California Bank, Fairmont Hotel Branch. Your Grand Lodge
Credentials will serve as suitable identification.
We wish to express our sincere appreciation to members of the Grand Lodge
Office Staff for their cooperation shown throughout the year in assembling,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON INSURANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge , F . & A. M. of California :
The Special Committee on Insurance continued to function in an ~dvisory capacity to the Grand Secretary and to be of aid to the Grand Master with regard to
Grand Lodge insurance matters.
The members of the Committee met to discuss and evaluate the current
insurance program for Grand Lodge and related entities. No new recommendations were made.
The " Loss Record Register" continues to be maintained and serves as a valuable tool to summarize losses that have occurred and permits corrective action to
be taken to reduce similar losses in the future.
The continued favorable loss experience with regard to Workmen's Compensation insurance resulted in a $32,829 dividend.
The Masonic Homes became self-insured with regard to unemployment
insurance. To reduce the possibility of a serious financial loss to Grand Lodge of
California in the event of a catastrophy, a ''Unemployment Reimbursement Coverage" policy was purchased.
. ..

maintaining our properties in a safe manner, thereby reducing the number of
losses .

GRAND ORATION
A FLICKERING FLAME?
WALKERS. KISSELBURGH, Grand Orator

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters,
distinguished guests and my Brethren:
Last year at this time you listened to an excellent Grand Oration en~i~led ''.The
Time is Now.'' This message stressed the point that there have been cnucal times

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

183

in our American Masonic History when our forefathers rose to the occasion and
brought our esteemed institution out of atmospheres of despair.
Let us, at this moment , continue on with this subject because one year later we
are still in a critical era so far as our honored fraternity is concerned . This critical
era concerns every one of us and we, like our forefathers, are going to have to do
what they did. They did not sit idly by and allow their ~onored fraterriity to die.
They rose to the occasion, rolled up their sleeves and went to work. In reality they
became "operative" Masons who built their Lodges.
Our Masonic forefathers have left us a tremendous heritage. The Masonic
heritage that we leave to our children and the Masons of the future should be held in
the same reverence with which we hold our Masonic forefathers.
The events that have transpired these past few months have shocked and
saddened all of us . We have seen men in our government who have abused their
power and thought they were above the law . And yet , as in the past, we will overcome these setbacks and go on to greater heights, because this is the American
way. Now, more than ever, we must arise to the occasion and provide leadership
- the likes we have never seen before.
Our fraternity, like our government, is indestructable and we will provide
leadership in our Lodges to continue this indestructability .
You Brethren sitting in the Grand Lodge Communication today are the ones to
whom we are addressing our remarks. You are the leaders of our Lodges and it is
on your shoulders that rests this tremendous responsibility of providing the leadership we need.
Our Lodges are crying out for inspired leadership. If you can provide it for
them, they will respond . They will respond so enthusiastically that you won't believe it.
To provideihis leadership, you must have confidence in your ability to lead .
You must pass on your enthusiasm and leadership to your junior officers so that
when they occupy the station of Worshipful Master, they will have been properly
indoctrinated.
My Brethren, along with leadership will come pride. Pride in your Lodge,
pride in your work and most important, pride in yourself. With pride and leadership you will be able to perform miracles. Our Masonic forefathers had a great
deal of pride in their Masonry and furnished leadership that is an inspiration to all
of us.
In the early days, the Masonic Lodge was the focal point or hub of social activities . And Masons looked forward to attending Lodge every week because they
enjoyed the fellowship and activities that it provided. However, this attendance
has suffered drastically this past 25 years due to competition from other interests.
And when these other interests become more important than the Lodge, then it is
only natural that our fraternity will suffer.
To improve attendance in your Lodge today is a mountainous task and yet it
must be done to stimulate the Masonic spirit and to keep our institution in a healthy
and enviable condition. This can be done with proper leadership. We must be constantly on the lookout for future leadership in our Lodges because it is most
important that we have continuing leadership. Not all members of our Lodges are
leaders, and we must make a diligent search for this leadership.

185

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Perhaps he might be a Brother who joined your Lodge several years ago and
was too busy to become a junior officer at the time he joined the Lodge. Contact
this brother and see if he is available today.
There have been isolated cases where a Brother was put into line as Senior
Deacon or Junior Warden, when he did not have eight or nine years to devote to his
Lodge as an officer because he was too busy at the time. Of course, this must be
done with the cooperation and complete harmony of your fellow officers. But the
important thing to remember, Brethren, is the best interest of your Lodge. If you
can get an outstanding Brother with excellent leadership qualities to agree to go
into the line and become Worshipful Master in three to four years, you should
make every effort to encourage him. This can be the first step in bringing your
Lodge up to its capabilities.
The second step deals with the most important word in the English language
- communication. Somehow, in the past, it has been communicated to us that
Masonry is a secret society and that all of our work is done in an atmosphere of
strict secrecy. First of all, let us remove from our minds that Masonry is a secret society. It is not. We must remove this stigma if our fraternity is to properly grow,
and Brethren, it must grow if it is to survive and remain in a healthy condition.
Let us go back, for a moment, to the coaching of our three degrees. If you
were like me, your coach impressed upon you that what you are learning should
not be revealed to anyone. Because you believed your coach, who most likely was
a newly raised Master Mason, you have not revealed anything to anyone. In other
words, we are never told what we can reveal, so for the fear of revealing something, we don't reveal anything.
Let each of us here in this great Grand Lodge pledge that we will educate ourselves so that we, the leaders, will be able to communicate with our Brethren especially the candidate's coach. Then they will be able to pass this communication on to the candidate. The Candidate's coach is the most important liaison
between the Lodge and the candidate. Let us do everything within our power to
remove the lid of secrecy concerning those Masonic tenets which are not esoteric.
In other words, if Freemasonry is good, let's talk about it. Past Grand Master
William H. Price, in his message to the 1973 Annual Grand Lodge Communication said in part, "there is so little about Masonry which is secret, I cannot
comprehend why this condition continues to prevail."
My Brethren, as you leave this hall you will be handed a pamphlet prepared by
our Past Grand Master Theodore Meriam, entitled, "If Freemasonry is good, let's
talk about it.'' Please, as leaders and future leaders of your Lodge, read this pamphlet. We urge you to distribute it to your members, especially your candidate's
coaches. Additional copies of this pamphlet may be obtained from the Grand Secretary's office. As leaders of your respective Lodges, you owe it to your
membership to educate them about what is secret and what is not. Let us all be
knowledgeable about what we can talk about regarding our institution.
This leads to the third step which is selling Freemasonry through our talk and
actions. In other words, once again, we must communicate. To be able to communicate is an art and we must be artists at our craft. And we must work at our craft today more than we have ever done in the past. In this day and age of electronic com-

munication, with the most sophisticated equipment ever divised by man, we
Masons must be able to communicate better with our fellow man regarding the
subject of Freemasonry. We must, if we are to survive as a fraternity .
Most of us are certainly knowledgeable about the fact that Masonry has been
on the decline for the past several decades. Yet, we are reluctant to do something
about it. Like our forefathers, we must accept the challenge, put our shoulders to
the wheel, and reverse this downward trend. Each one of us must accept the
responsibility of keeping our age old fraternity in a healthy and prosperous
condition. We can do this by communicating about Freemasonry. The foundation
of Masonry is that you must be a good man to become a member. However, not all
good men are Masons. We, therefore, are not communicating with these good
men.
In our communications we must put across these several points. Number one
-you will not be asked to become a Mason. How many times have we heard men
say: "I would have become a Mason long ago but I was waiting to be asked."
Number two - Our fraternity is not a religious organization . Our one and only
religious requirement is that you must believe in a Supreme Being. Number three
- Our fraternity is not a secret organization. There are many things that we can
discuss outside of the Lodge room. For example, we can discuss with anyone that
our organization stands for everything that is good. The teachings of our craft
should be well known to everyone - but in order for this to happen, we must communicate. However, in our communication we must be completely understood.
Remember what happened to the village blacksmith who was holding a horseshoe
with both hands and told his not-too-bright son- ''when I nod my head, son, hit it
with a hammer." My Brethren; this is communication but it is misunderstood. Let
us not have any misunderstanding in our communications about Freemasonry.
Talking as.Masons and acting as Masons is the most important way to get a
friend or an acquaintance of yours to say: "How do I become a Mason?" or "I
want to be a Mason."
We are judged by our words and actions. Therefore, let us, everyone of us,
know by our words and actions that we are Masons .
Talk about your Lodge - brag about your Masonic beliefs. Let everyone
know that all Masons are good men, and that we make better men out of these good
men. Let everyone know that you stand for the brotherhood of man under the fatherhood of God. In communicating with our friends, our next door neighbors, our
casual acquaintances, we can be so enthusiastic about being a Mason, that it could
trigger a chain of events. Because you are proud and because you enjoy Masonry
so much, and mostly by your upright and outstanding conduct, your exposure to
your friends or neighbors could stimulate a desire in them to become Masons.
Therefore, we must constantly communicate. Know what you can talk about.
Knowledge is power. Our great Masonic fraternity can be a powerful influence in
the future, just like it has been in the past.
Masonry is the foundation of our government; Our Masonic forefathers, who
were the signers of the Declaration of Independence, made sure that that document
contained our Masonic principles. This famous document has survived for two
centuries and just recently was tested and found to be unshakeable. It has proven
resilient, able to survive and eventually overcome the ordeal of recent scandals.

186

187

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Many of our government leaders of today are Masons, and as long as we have
that kind of leadership in our country, there is hope and trust that our government
will endure. No other form of government has endured this long. And if we the
people become concerned about good government- then we can endure for many
more centuries to come. Our government may not be perfect, but it is the best that
man has ever devised.
In closing, my Brethren, let me emphasize the seriousness of the situation.
We must stop the declining membership and we must furnish our Lodges with
inspired leadership. All over these great United States we are faced with the same
problem. If our wonderful Masonic fraternity is to continue, we must, each one of
us, pledge ourselves to do everything that we can possibly do to improve its
condition. Let us, like our Masonic forefathers, make sure that the flickering flame
of Freemasonry once again becomes a bright beacon for those who follow us.
Thank you.

REPORT OF THE BICENTENNIAL COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California

Upon taking office in the Fall of 1973, the Most Worshipful Grand Masterof
the Grand Lodge of California, Raymond A. Ebbage, reappointed the following
Paster Masters (who have served since the Committee's inception in 1972) to continue to serve upon the Grand Lodge Bicentennial Committee: Lester S. McElwain
(403, Past Grand Master, Chairman, Elmer P. Bromley (698), Richard H. Chamberlain (521), WalterW. Powers (579), and Edward G. Van Pelt (778). The Grand
Master, also, appointed Donald Ingalls, Past Master of North Hollywood Lodge,
No. 542, and William Lambert, Past Master of Nevada Lodge, No. 13, as additional members of the Committee. The Senior Grand Warden, Right Worshipful
John F. Roberts, Jr., also was again appointed as the Committee's Liaison Officer
with the elective California Grand Lodge line of officers. Worshipful Brother Donald Ingalls previously had been serving as a consultant to the Committel~.
All of the Committee members have worked long and well together during the
past year, and each has carried out his assignment promptly and effectively.
The purpose of this Committee was and is to encourage the Craft Lodges in our
jurisdiction to recognize the importance of and now plan a program for a
celebration in 1976 of the two hundredth anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence from England on July 4, 1776. This great document was
drafted and signed by many of our earlier Brother Masons.
No Masonic Bicentennial Program in 1976 commemorating that great event is
contemplated upon a national basis; for the Conference of Grand Masters of North
American previously determined in 1969 and 1970 that each Grand Lodge
jurisdiction should be responsible for and conduct its own program for appropriate
Bicentennial celebrations during 1976.
The members of your Committee believe that, in accordance with the purpose
for which the Committee was appointed, the members thereof should work closely

The San Bernardino Scottish Rite Bodies is planning to present its patriotic

and all Masons and their friends will be and are invited to attend;
The California Scottish Rite Bodies of San Francisco have arranged to present

great event of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, and he and those
Scottish Rite Bodies are already formulating plans to that effect;
The Long Beach Scottish Rite Bodies are planning and hope in 1976 to have its
degree team simulate in costumes of the times the First Degree of Masonry as it
was conferred on Brother George Washington on November 4, 1752, at
Fredericksburg, Virginia;
The Al Malaikah Shrlne Temple of Los Angeles is planning many Bicentennial

The new Editor-In-Chief of the California Freemason, Ralph H. Head, Past

The Grand Chaplain, Dr. Earl C. Evans, has suggested that all of us Accent the
Positive and look at the good in individuals, institutions, and our Country. In other
words he suggests that we recognize, stress and publicize the good things and
many benefits the Constitution and our form of government give to all of our people; and also we should be sure to encourage others to look for the good in America
and praise it. Of course all is not perfect; but there is so much that is praise-worthy
- let's all talk about and praise the many good things in America.
After this communication, in early November of this year, another joint letter is
planned to be sent to all present Senior Wardens (the incoming Masters) by the
then Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master and the chairman of the Bicentennial
Committee urging the incoming Masters to bring their Bicentennial plans to an appropriate conclusion in 1975, so as to be ready for an exciting charge upon the
planned program in 1976.
Finally and in conclusion your Committee's plans for an outstanding and
inspiring celebration of the Bicentennial event in Los Angeles on Sunday, July 4,
1976, are continuing to develop well. The Los Angeles Sports Arena (near the Los
Angeles Coliseum where ample parking for vehicles is available) has been
reserved and leased forouruse onJuly4, 1976. ThereducedrentoftheSports Arena on this occasion is $3,000.00, and one-half of that sum already has been paid to
assure its use by us on that date. The balance of the rental charge will be paid at a
later date. This Sports Arena will comfortably accommodate between 16,000 and
17 ,000 persons, and we anticipate that it will be filled on this occasion, for we believe that our program on July 4, 1976, will be outstanding. There will be no admission charge, and all Masons, their families, Concordant Bodies, and friends
will be welcome and urged to attend. We should have a very pleasant, interesting
and exciting fraternal gathering there with our Brethren and friends, for we expect
the Sports Arena to be filled to capacity with standing room only for those who
arrive late.
The program has been entitled "Freedom On Trial" and is being written,
produced, and directed by our own Don Ingalls, Past Master of North Hollywood
Lodge, No. 542, a top motion picture producer and director, whom you will recall
gave us that beautiful inspiring talking motion picture about our great Masonic
fraternity entitled, "Journey Into Truth." Those of you who have heard and viewed this fine talking film know of the high caliber of Don's work, which assures us
that the July 4, 1976 Los Angeles Bicentennial Program will be outstanding and
thoroughly enjoyed by all who see it.
"Freedom On Trial" will be a program put together in an exciting manner
depicting events and dealing with, in chronological order, various important

episodes which occurred in the development and throughout the history of our
Country, the United States of America. Those participating in the program will be
dressed in the clothes and costumes of the times in an effort to capture the spirit and
attitude of those great individuals who gave so much of themselves in their efforts
for their Country, our Nation, which now is our great and wonderful heritage.
Life in a struggling America, and even up to modem times, often was and is not
easy, and we must never forget that Freedom is never easy - it is always on trial;
but in this Country under God's benign blessing, Freedom (while often forced to
strUggle) has flourished and always triumphed. However, in order to have
freedom, we must always remember that continual vigilance is required to insure
that the torch-light of freedom never goes out, for Freedom is always on trial- we
can loose it, if we are not vigilant. Thank God for Masonry, its members and
principles; for Masons always have been in the vanguard to uphold the rights of the
individual and Freedom for all, no matter what the effort or trial involved.
The Committee requests a budget of $3 ,600. 00 to carry on its work during the
coming Masonic year.

IJ.EPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
TO PREPARE GRAND LODGE HISTORY PUBLICATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In 1971 Grand Master Herbert A. Huebner recommended that a comprehensive

history be compiled centering around the Grand Lodge and that it cover the 125year period 1850 to 1975. He further suggested that the history be published in
time for the Bicentennial Celebration of the United States in 1976.
The Committee has completed the final draft of the manuscript covering the
years through 1973. The events of 1974 and 1975 will be written and included in
the completed publication.
The 300-page·volume has been written in easy-to-read style and covers many
outstanding events in the development of our Fraternity and the unselfish contributions of its leaders. Numerous historical pictures and documents are being
processed and are to be interspersed throughout the book.
The first printing is to be limited to 2000 copies and will be available at our next
Annual Communication in October 1975.
The production costs have been estimated to be $10.00 to $12.00 per copy and it
is expected that this cost will be offset by income from sales.
We are grateful to Most Worshipful Raymond A. Ebbage and his Officers for
their encouragement and assistance in this project.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Since Grand Lodge has been shortened by one day this year, I will make this report as brief as possible.
The slogan for Public Schools Month this past year was "Public Education the Foundation of Democracy" and was well received. The slogan chosen by the
Deputy Grand Master for the coming year is "Public Schools - Freedom's First
Fronter" and we trust that this will be equally well received.
During the past year there was a tremendous increase in the number of pamphlets furnished to the Lodges when 131,747 were distributed. In addition, 2,347
certificates of appreciation were presented by the constituent Lodges.
On the legislative front we had great support from a three judge Federal Court
declaring California's Parochial Law AB 1724 unconstitutional. This law would
have provided for a tax credits of from $25. 00 to $125. 00 per pupil in religious and
other private schools. Further rockets could have been sent up in June of this year
when the Supreme Court further limited State aid to parochial schools.
We must not relax, Brethren as these bills to aid non-public schools will be
coming up to the Legislature with increasing frequency.
For the second year we, as a Committee, asked the Lodges to complete a report
on their public schools observance and the similarity of the results is almost
identical:

These statistics point out our long-standing assertion that the earlier a Lodge begins planning the better its chances of having a more successful observanc~.
Brethren, give your Lodge a chance. Begin early to plan your successful Pubhc
School Observance.
The Committee is still committed 100% to changing back from Public Schools
Month to Public Schools Week and has introduced Resolution No. 2. You will
hear more about this at the proper time.

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
YOUTH ACTIVITIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Grand Lodge Youth Activities Committee held two meetings during the
current year. The first meeting was held July 20, 1974 in San Diego for members
residing in the Southern part of the State. The second meeting was held on September 7, 1974 in San Francisco for members of the northern part of the
jurisdiction. The meetings were held separately to keep expenses to a minimum.
At the meeting in San Diego 12 members and the chairman were in attendance.
The San Francisco meeting was attended by 9 members and the chairman.
The Committee during its discussion, repeatedly emphasized the need for the
Grand Master to clearly state the purpose and goals of the Committee on Youth Activities as they would reflect the goals of Freemasonry in California. The Committee felt that merely to offer assistance to the Order of DeMolay, International Order
of Rainbow for Girls and the International Order of Jobs Daughters provided
insufficient direction for the achievement of any productive objectives. The
chairman encouraged that each committeemen use his own initiative in holding
communication with Masonic District Inspectors, Youth Group Advisory Boards,
Blue Lodges and other sponsoring bodies. It was stressed that Grand Lodge
resources could not be committed without explicit authorization.

195

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Committe e agreed that a resolution calling for full recognitio n of Jobs
Daughter s and Rainbow for Girls should be submitted for adoption at the 1975
Grand Lodge Commun ication, inasmuch as it was too late to submit same for the
current year. The Chairman also noted that Most Worshipful Raymond A. Ebbage
had stated that a similar proposal would be forthcomi ng from him at this year's
Communi cation at Grand Lodge.
Richard Kelly, Director of Activities Southern Jurisdicti on, Order of De Mo lay,
acted as a consultan t to the Committe e meeting in San Diego. He stated that
DeMolay chapters in San Diego County did not require financial assistance . Numerous letters have been received by the chairman that fees charged to the youth.
groups in some temples are exhorbitant. In some cases discussio ns held with the
Master of the Lodge have been successful in securing assistance for the youth
group, in others, especially where Temple Boards are involved, we are informed
that the problem still exists. A letter from our Most Worshipful Grand Master,
referring to rental fees, was mailed to all constitue nt Lodges during the year.
A Mini Ritual, copy of which was mailed to Right Worshipf ul H. Douglas
Lemons, Grand Lecturer, was prepared and presentation of same to the Youth
Groups was recomme nded. This would encourag e officers of the Lodges involved
to attend meetings of the Youth Groups, to exemplify the permissib le portions of
the degree. The idea was enthusiastically received by the youth groups which had
been approached also by the committe emen. This idea had also been previously
discussed with Most Worshipf ul Raymond A. Ebbage. The wholehea rted support
of Grand Lodge, given to our three youth groups, was discussed and praised. It
was felt that our Grand Masters, particularly during the past years, have spent a
great deal of energy to encourag e individual Masons as well as Lodges to lend a
helping hand to our youth which are the future members of the Fraternity.
At the meeting in San Diego it was requested that the chairman mail copies of
the Grand Master's Message 1971, regarding the youth groups, as stated by Most
Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner P.G.M. Copies have been reprinted and will go
out to members of the Committe e. Likewise , copies of the membersh ip roster will
be mailed to each Committe eman.
An invitation to the Committe e, extended by Lester McElwain P.G.M., to actively participate in the Bi-Centennial Celebrati on was discussed . It was felt that
our Committe e did not have a useful function in this matter as the Youth Groups
have already been approach ed to participate in the Blue Lodge programs . It was
therefore decided to decline this invitation and to confine ourselves to the purposes
of our own work.
The Committe e voted on lowering the age limit from 21 to 18 years, in order to
make a recomme ndation. The combined vote of the two meetings was 17 opposed,
4 in favor and one abstention. It was agreed that leadership training for our youth
should be promoted . The chairman asked each member to take the DeMolay leadership course. Applications will be provided by brother Richard Kelley.
The chairman was going to try to have an article published in the California
Freemaso n admonish ing Masons to support our youth groups by attending their
meetings. Sincerity and visible interest should be displayed.

It seems that the meetings of the Committe e inspired everyone to work diligently toward the common goal of assisting our youth groups in whatever capacity
was requested by them. We should approach them, not wait for them to ask us. It
was hoped that the Committe e would be much the same for the ensuing year, as we
have only been able to lay ground rules during the present one.
Respectfully submitted ,

REPORT OF TAXATION COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:

Your Committee on Taxation was originally appointed in the l930's to deal
with problems having to do with the social security_law~. and in 197 l ~ran~ ~ge
expanded its function to "include all types oftaxat10n. YourCo~m1tt~ i_s without authority to supervise tax activities within Grand Lodge ?11d its entities and
considers itself an advisory committee available for consultation on tax matters.
The primary responsibility for dealing with tax matters is that o~ the Gr~~ Master
and Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge, the truste~s of the vai:ious entities of the
Grand Lodge, the Worshipful Masters and Secn:tanes of consutu~nt Lodges, and
elected or appointed officers and trustees of vanous other Masomc groups under
.

the Grand Lodge.
Most units of Grand Lodge with employees are involved with Federal social
security and California unemployment and disability insurance laws. Grand Lodge

199

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and its entities are also involved with a wide range of Federal and California laws
pertaining to tax exempt organizations and also to other laws such as taxation of
associations, corporations, fiduciaries, pension funds, and sales taxes. Much of
the law involved is dynamic with frequent changes, new regulations, and
increasing enforcement. The laws are complex and difficult of interpretation.
Very substatial assets are entailed. Required returns are subject to ever more critical review and audit.
Your Committee strongly advises that all those responsible recognize this is
an area beyond casual consideration. It urges that advice be solicited and consultation be made with legal and accounting professionals as well as your Committee. Your Committee recommends that each Grand Lodge unit establish a program
for active review of the requirements of the various tax laws so that there will be
continual compliance with these laws. Failure to comply with the law can subject
our organizations to costly penalties and the Fraternity to embarrassment.
Your Committee suggests that all Brethren take the responsibility of
determining full compliance with the tax laws of our nation and state. It believes
this to be a duty of every elected presiding officer and trustee from the Grand
Master to the Master of the Lodge, from the trustee of the Grand Lodge Homes,
Temple, and Foundation to the trustees of the Temple Associations and from the
officers of Service Bureaus, Masters and Wardens Associations, and Secretaries
Associations to the trustees of pension funds and separate Lodge funds.
Your Committee again reminds the brethren that tax laws are the law of the
land and as good citizens we must comply with the law. We have been granted tax
exemptions in many cases and it is our duty to be worthy of that advantage.

We know that California Masonic History began with the formation of Grand
l,odge in April 1850, 5 lodges, 567 members in total. It has been duly recorded in
numerous articles and publications, the most noteworthy being "One Hundred
Years of Freemasonry in California" by Brother Leon Whitsell. While Brother
Whitsell is our most illustrous recorder of Masonic history, I submit that he also
made history himself. For over 30 years he roamed the state, visiting lodges and
old Lodge-Sites, collecting material, searching into the past. What appears in the
printed set is but a small fraction of the total.
The Masonic History Committee had its beginning in 1925 with the recommendation of and subsequent appointment by the Grand Master of a ''Committee of 3
members for the Preservation of Masonic History in California under the leadership of a Masonic Historian." A rather elaborate structure was discussed in
1926, calling for a Grand Historian, and 3 Deputy Grand Historians, with 3
depositories in the state. This proposal apparently died of its own weight.
In 1927 the name of Brother Whitsell appears for the first time as a member of
the Committee, and he became Chairman in 1932. In those early days the Committee aimed for the publication of a California History, planned then to consist of 3
volumnes and to be sold by subscription to the Brethem for $12.00 per set. But the
great depression was upon us, and out of some 2000 letters sent out to Lodges and
members, only 324 signed up. As a consequence the project was abandoned for the
time being. But Grand Lodge adopted as policy that the History Committee "work
out the most feasable and economic plan for the preparation and publication of the
History of Masonry in California.'' As we know it was finally published as a part
of our centennial in 1950.
We were indeed fortunate to have had a most ardent and hardworking historian
to guide the project. Restoration of the Temple at Columbia, our slide presentation, numerous Qther proposals came from his boundless energy. His footsteps
may be traced throughout the Mother Lode country as well as other places of Masonic consequence. Even when elected Deputy Grand Master, he carried on with
the Committee activities, severing his membership and chairmanship only for the
year he was Grand Master in 1938. Upon relinquishing that office, he immediately
returned to the History Committee and again became its chairman. The publication
of the '100 years' for our centennial is well known to all.
Our Masonic History is the story of the lives of all of us, told individually and
collectively from 1850 until now. But as you read the printed words, do you let
yourself become for a moment a part of that past history? Imagine yourself as one
of the officers of those 5 original lodges; your dress, working mens clothing, tom,
faded and full of patches; meetings held in crudely constructed and ill-furnished
Lodge rooms. Picture the communication system then, if you will, and the streets
you walked to get to the Lodge room. And transportation? - no paved roads,
freeways, much less jets traveling at 600 miles per hour. We complain today at the
new 55 miles per hour speed limit on the highways. But consider the problem of
Brother Levi Stowell, Master of California Lodge No. 1 in 1850. He was then a
member of the state legislature, meeting at that time in San Jose some 50 miles to
the south of San Francisco. Faithfuly, by stage coach he travelled for 6 to 8 hours in
order to be able to come to San Francisco and open his beloved Lodge.

Respectfully submitted,
W. STANLEY DAVIS, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

What is History? It is the story of what happened today-yesterday. We are all
makers of and a part of history, even though not necessarily recorded. Most of it is
lost to posterity, only a few of the more important events finding their way into the
printed page.

200

201

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Ritualist work may have left much to be desired, but they were Masons in truth
and in fact. These handful of Masons, totaling 567 in 1851, contributed out of their
own pockets the sum of $34,000 during 1850 and 1851 for the relief of needy
Brothers during a disaster in Sacramento. Grand Lecturers and Inspectors unknown then, although by the end of 25 years in 1874 we numbered 27 district
Inspectors.
Gold is much in the news today. History tells us that in 1874 our Brethern in
Louisiana were greatly in need of help and relief, and we raised funds here in
California to send to them. "Gold drafts" were purchased in San Francisco for
$2,500.00, realizing for our Louisiana Brethern the sum of $2,748.75.
And still on the subject of finances, we learned that the cost of operating our
Fraternity was of great concern. Grand Lodge dues were said to be too high, and
the proceedings report ''on this subject, more feeling has been exhibited and more
comments expended than on any other topic."
Such are bits of Masonic history, interesting to some, to be ignored by others.
In 1960, each constituent lodge received a letter from the History Committee
headed by Brother Whitsell, requesting information to gather the story of
Freemasonry in California after 1950. He asked for the recording of events within
each Lodge such as anniversaries and centennials; Lodge dedications; new
Temples, mortgage burnings, to name a few. It must regretfully be reported that
one year later, only 96 Lodges complied with his request in detail, 114 were
partially answered, and sad to say 476 Lodges did not reply at all. Since that time
another request has gone out but still only scattered responses have been received.
History recording is a never ending mission. The History Committee should be
writiQg our history as it is being made, day by day. Brother Whitsell continued his
search for further Masonic material until 1962, when he filed a final report with
Grand Lodge after 30 years of service.
In order to preserve our heritage, much remains to be accomplished. We must
consolidate what we have, and bring all the records up to date. The history files today are incomplete, and what information we do have is scattered in different
spots. It had been our hope this year that we could bring all of the information
concerning each Lodge into a single file folder for that Lodge, and keep it up to
date by a constant flow of new material coming to us. At the present time we have
numerical Lodge files; chronological files containing some Lodge history; scrap
books of old Lodge temples and interior halls; cases of individual file folders on the
floor which should be consolidated with the numerical files; information in the
Grand Secretary's office and records which should be cross filed in the history section; and we suspect even the records of the California Freemason will reveal pertinent information of historical interest.
It will take time and physical effort to consolidate all of this scattered information into one place. But it is of extreme importance, for without a central source for
complete information about each Lodge, the second century of our history will be
lost.
That is not all to be done however. The active support of each individual Lodge
is essential. Future History Committees will undoubtedly be requesting reports
from you. Let each one of us resolve today to go back to our respective Lodges and

become ourselves "Historians," preserving our glorious past and building for the
future.
Respectfully submitted,
PAUL COWGILL, Chairman
ROBERT L. HIRT
FRED 0. SHERRILL

WILLIAM NADEL

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
TO STUDY FEASIBILITY OF FREEMASON AS
MONTHLY PUBLICATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In his message to Grand Lodge at the last Communication, Grand Master
William H. Price made the observation that there is "need for more communication between the Grand Master (or Grand Lodge) and those members who
cannot or do not regularly attend Lodge meetings." He concluded his remarks
with the hope that the California Freemason magazine would be published
monthly and recommended a special committee to determine the advisability and
feasibility.
This Committee believes that it is both possible and feasible to publish the
California Freemason monthly.
Any recommendation as to advisability must take into account the impact of
increased costs. Now published quarterly, the California Freemason is paid for by
means of an annual assessment on each Lodge at the rate of 35¢ per member. An
examination of the latest costs indicates that this assessment approximately equals
the present cost.
Publication expense is divided into ( l) the updating of the mailing list which
requires the time of one Grand Lodge employee, (2) the actual printing costs, (3)
cost of processing mailing labels and postage expense, and (4) editorial costs.
Two-thirds of the total expense is in the printing of the magazine which includes
paper, an item which can be expected to increase in the future, along with postage.
· The Committee believes that the total cost would probably increase in almost
direct proportion to the number of issues. Therefore, any reasonable projection
indicates that issuing the Californis Freemason on a monthly basis would require
an assessment on each Lodge of approximately $1.15 per member compared with
the present 35¢. Reducing the size of the magazine would effect some savings,
but would not materially affect the assessment.
The Committee believes that planned changes will make the magazine into
even a better means of communication with all members. Nonetheless, we are
reluctant to recommend publication on a monthly basis because of the increased
financial burden which would result.
Respectfully submitted,
JOHN A. SICKENBERGER, Chairman
LLOYD A. BUDWIG

RALPH H. HEAD

The report lists two conclusions or opinions; the first is that the Study Committee believes that ''planned changes will make the magazine into even a

what "planned changes" are contemplated, we trust that all such planned
changes would upgrade the present high quality of the California

Policy and General Purposes that a more frequent publication of the
California Freemason would tend toward a possible lowering of the
quality. It is further believed that greater attention will be given to a quality
quarterly publication than to a monthly or bi-monthly periodical.

to recommend a monthly publication because of increased financial
burden. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes wholeheartedly
concurs with the Study Committee in this respect and further suggests that
if additional funds should become available they should be used for expansion of the present quarterly into an even larger, more complete publication. It is the belief of your committee that the brethren of this

the elected Grand Lodge officers (both as to Masonic service and coriununity service) and in all offerings that tend to strengthen our quality as an
institution and to increase individual pride in membership.

communication link between the Grand Lodge and the individual Mason.

The Committee on Finance has studied the Report of the Special Committee as
to the possibility of publishing the Freemason magazine on a monthly basis.

magazine monthly could be approximately $250,000.00. This is an addition of
